sources.news_title: "My Dad Was Watching"
sources.text:
James Forman Jr. watched Scott Colom claim victory as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since 1881 — and he couldn’t stop thinking of his own father.
That would be the late civil rights leader James Forman. James Forman Sr. made history in Mississsippi 62 summers ago by helping organize civil rights workers who risked (and in some cases lost) their lives to restore Black Americans’ right to vote and participate in democracy.
Colom’s victory was a culmination of that work.
“I have been on cloud nine” since Colom’s victory was called Wednesday night, Forman, a Yale law professor and Pulitzer Prize-winning author, said Thursday, hours after the announcement of Colom’s victory.
“I grew up with stories of what Mississippi life was like for” his father, Forman said during a conversation on WNHH FM’s “Dateline New Haven.”
The stories included the dirt his father ate as a young boy growing up in Mississippi, along with the racial oppression and violence he witnessed.
Americans have heard the later stories that became part of our historical canon: How Forman Sr. served as executive secretary of the Student Nonviolence Coordinating Committee (SNCC). How SNCC organized an interracial group of volunteers from around the country to descend on Mississippi for a “Freedom Summer” campaign seeking to win the state’s majority Black population to vote. How volunteers were murdered, imprisoned, while segregationists burned and bombed Black businesses and homes.
The election of Democrat Colom in a state his party had written off as unwinnable marked a new milestone in the series of staccato civil rights advances that followed Freedom Summer.
Forman Jr. recalled on “Dateline” that his father was still in Ohio training Freedom Summer volunteers when activists James Chaney, Michael Schwerner, and Andrew Goodman went missing.
“The SNCC staff in Mississippi had to call up to Ohio and to tell everybody, ‘Hey, listen, three of you have disappeared. And we know enough about Mississippi that we have to be honest. We don’t think they’re alive.’
“All these volunteers are still in training, and almost to a person, they all still decided to go. That is the kind of of sacrifice that people were making.”
Forman, who is 59, has continued the civil rights work of his parents. His years as a public defender informed his groundbreaking book about the racial complexities of the drug war, Locking Up Our Own: Crime and Punishment in Black America. He has created programs to widen the group of people able to attend law school and bring legal education into prisons. He has worked on protests and worked with East Rock neighbors to support progressive campaigns nationwide.
He noted that while Freedom Summer drew volunteers from around the country, SNCC leaders like his father understood the centrality of long-term locally based grassroots political work. That made a difference in Colom’s history victory, Forman Jr. argued.
“This election is really a story of local organizing. Scott Colom talked about that. I don’t think there’s any question that this victory would not have come, but for the Civil Rights Movement, but for Fannie Lou Hamer, but for SNCC, but for Medgar Evers, and but for all of the people that have marched in their shoes.”
He noted that Republican efforts to eliminate Black majority districts through Supreme Court-enabled gerrymanders produced a backlash among Black voters who voted in numbers usually seen only in presidential years.
But Forman also noted that a confluence of one-time factors — like that gerrymandering and widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration — threaten to make the Nov. 3 election victories a one-off.
So he called for political actors to heed a second lesson from Colom’s victory: showing up everywhere to talk to all kinds of voters, not just the people who agree with you or districts you think you’ve drawn.
Surprise victories like Colom’s throughout the South in the Nov. 3 election upended conventional strategy by both parties to focus on gerrymandering districts and focusing campaigns on the base that already supports them. Forman noted the importance of Colom even attending a rally Donald Trump held on behalf of Colom’s Republican opponent.
He’d like to see both parties embrace nonpartisan commissions to draw voting districts that replace gerrymanders.
In the meantime, veterans of the Civil Rights Movement and their descendants are still savoring Colom’s victory as the pinnacle of a wave of stunning victories (in Kansas, Michigan, Georgia, Ohio, South Carolina) that reignited hope.
Forman took note of the movement veterans he watched gathering in Mississippi Wednesday night to celebrate Colom’s win.
“I’m not a big religious person,” Forman said. “But I know that my dad was watching.”

sources.news_title: Trump won Mississippi by 23 points — now GOP Sen concedes to Democrat in historic upset
sources.text:
The Mississippi Senate race took a surprising turn as a Republican incumbent endorsed by President Donald Trump conceded the race to her Democratic rival.
In another Democrat upset in the Deep South, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded to Scott Colom Wednesday, making the Democrat the first in his party to be elected to the state’s Senate seat since 1982.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith, who was looking to be re-elected, said in a video message. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Colom, the District Attorney for the 16th Circuit Court, “becomes Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction,” Axios noted, adding that “Mississippi’s last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881.”
Hyde-Smith said her campaign “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”
“I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will,” she said.

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” the 43-year-old district attorney told a crowd of supporters at a victory party on Wednesday. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

sources.news_title: Democrat Scott Colom flips a Mississippi Senate seat Trump carried by more than 20 points
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on November 3, 2026; the Associated Press confirmed the result eight days later after a full tally of mail-in, provisional, and affidavit ballots.
- Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black U.S. Senator since Blanche Kelso Bruce left office in 1881 and the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate seat since 1982 — the same year Colom was born.
- The victory pushes Democrats to at least 55 Senate seats — their largest upper-chamber majority in more than a decade — with a race in Alaska still unresolved.
A Democrat just won a United States Senate seat in a state Donald Trump carried by more than 20 points two years ago — and the final margin may come down to fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million cast.
Scott Colom, a 43-year-old District Attorney for Mississippi's 16th Judicial District, unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on November 3, 2026, in the most consequential upset of a midterm cycle already defined by Democratic momentum. The Associated Press made its call on November 11 — eight days after polls closed — following a meticulous count of outstanding mail-in and provisional ballots.
The result reshapes the U.S. Senate map in ways no major political forecaster had anticipated.
The Man Who Turned a Personal Snub Into a Senate Campaign
Scott Colom describes himself as a seventh-generation Mississippian. Born on December 24, 1982, in Columbus — just weeks after the last Democrat won a Senate seat in the state — he earned a double-major undergraduate degree from Millsaps College and a law degree cum laude from the University of Wisconsin Law School. After graduating, he returned home, became Columbus's first Black city prosecutor, and was sworn in on January 4, 2016, as District Attorney for the 16th Judicial District, making him the first Black DA ever elected in a majority-white Mississippi district.
His path to the Senate runs directly through a grievance against the very senator he unseated. In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination to a federal district court judgeship by withholding the senatorial blue slip required to advance his confirmation. Colom said at the time that what stung him was not the rejection itself, but the process — he had been given no hearing and no voice in the matter. That episode, by his own account, turned a prosecutor's career into a Senate campaign.
His biography carries a cross-partisan texture unusual for a Democrat running in the Deep South. His father campaigned for Ronald Reagan and counted the late Republican Sen. Thad Cochran among his friends. Colom built his coalition by cultivating both the Black voters who anchor the Democratic base and persuadable Republicans — including former Republican governors and allies of Sen. Roger Wicker.
A Platform Anchored in Kitchen-Table Economics, Not Ideology
Colom ran not on party orthodoxy but on tangible financial relief for working Mississippians. His signature proposal calls for eliminating federal income taxes on teachers and law enforcement officers earning under $75,000 annually — a policy he refined after speaking with a single mother working two jobs in south Mississippi. He called consistently for raising the federal minimum wage, arguing that Hyde-Smith had cast votes that left Mississippi workers behind. On rural health care — a crisis-level concern in a state where several hospitals have shuttered in recent years — he pledged to restore Medicaid funding and fight further closures, framing the issue as life-or-death rather than partisan. He also pointed to the 2021 Jackson water crisis as direct evidence of the cost of voting against federal infrastructure investment, a pointed reference to Hyde-Smith's opposition to the Bipartisan Infrastructure Act.
As a DA who built his record pursuing violent crime while prioritizing rehabilitation for non-violent offenders, Colom offered a more pragmatic approach to criminal justice than the progressive wing of his party typically endorses. Throughout the race, he deliberately rejected ideological framing: "At the end of the day, you've got to put Mississippi above D.C. politics," he said — a posture that may prove essential for governing in a state that voted for Trump by double digits.
The Arithmetic That Made a Miracle Possible
Strategists who had studied Mississippi's demographics argued that Colom needed to push Black turnout to roughly 35 percent of the electorate — above historical norms — while winning closer to one-in-four white voters rather than the customary one-in-five. Mississippi Today reported that Colom rode strong support in majority-Black counties to close the gap against an incumbent who had won reelection by nearly 10 percentage points in 2020.
At one moment on election night, the gap between the two candidates stood at just 36 votes out of approximately 920,000 ballots cast — less than a hundredth of a percent. As late-arriving mail and provisional ballots were processed over the following week, Colom's lead widened steadily until the AP confirmed him as the winner on Veterans Day, by which point he led by approximately 4,669 votes.
Hyde-Smith's Liability: An Absent Incumbent
The Republican senator carried a structural vulnerability into the race: she had not held a public town hall since first taking office, a contrast Colom hammered at every turn. Hyde-Smith had won the seat through appointment in 2018, survived a competitive runoff that year, and cruised to reelection in 2020 — but she entered the 2026 campaign weighed down by her vote against the Bipartisan Infrastructure Act, her refusal to certify the 2020 presidential election results, and consumer frustration with rising costs, which Colom's campaign channeled into the nickname "Cindy High Prices."
After the final count was confirmed, Hyde-Smith released a video statement: "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters." Her campaign confirmed she had called Colom to offer her personal congratulations.
The Bigger Picture: Democrats Control Both Chambers
NBC News projects Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats — their strongest position in the upper chamber since the early Obama years — with the Alaska contest still awaiting a final call. CBS News confirmed Colom's win as the party's eighth Senate flip of the cycle, following victories in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and Maine. Democrats also appear to have recaptured the House of Representatives, with NBC projecting at least 258 seats to Republicans' 176, giving the party full legislative control heading into a confrontation with the White House over budget priorities, health care, and foreign policy.
For Senate Democrats, Mississippi closes a midterm cycle that party strategists will study for years. Colom himself acknowledged the late arrival of national party investment in his race, crediting a surge of support from figures including former Vice President Kamala Harris and Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks with keeping his campaign competitive in its final weeks. For Republicans, losing a state Trump won by more than 20 points sets off a reckoning over candidate quality, voter engagement, and the limits of the coalition Senate Majority Leader John Thune had been counting on to hold power.
A Historic Night on a Historic Campus
Colom delivered his victory speech Wednesday night at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi — a historically Black institution whose roots run deep into the American civil rights movement — before a crowd of supporters who understood the full weight of the moment. His address saluted that movement explicitly.
The last Black senator to represent Mississippi, Blanche Kelso Bruce, left office in 1881. The last Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate race did so in 1982 — the year Colom was born.
"I kept the faith," Colom told the crowd.
The state certification deadline is November 13, 2026.

sources.news_title: ‘The View’: Sunny Hostin Delights in the ‘Karma’ of Scott Colom Winning Mississippi Senate Race
sources.text:
After days of counting, Scott Colom was officially projected to win the senate race in Mississippi this week, and the hosts of “The View” were thrilled to see it. But host Sunny Hostin took particular joy in the “karma” of the results.
Colom ran against Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, and became Mississippi’s first black senator in 150 years. It’s a massive win for Democrats in a sea of unexpected wins this year, but it’s also a bit of payback for Colom, in the eyes of Hostin.
“He was the district attorney in in Mississippi. She blocked his appointment as a federal judge,” Hostin explained. “Joe Biden nominated him to be a federal judge. She blocked that appointment, and then four years later, [Colom] came back and blocked her! It was just sort of the karma of it all.”
Meanwhile, host Joy Behar pointed out the historical context of the counties that Colom won.
“He flipped what’s called Forrest County, which was named for the Ku Klux Klan’s first Grand Wizard, Nathan Bedford Forrest,” she detailed. “He flipped that district that was named after a Klansman. Colom won also Jefferson Davis County, named after the Confederate president, President Jefferson. Unbelievable.”
Hostin also stressed that Colom is proof that deep red states don’t always have to stay that way.
“You’ve got to believe that that people can win in the South. That we can take the South,” she said. “That was important.”
“The View” airs weekdays at 11 a.m. ET on ABC.

sources.news_title: Black voters view Scott Colom's historic US Senate win through lens of Mississippi's racial legacy
sources.text:
It's been nearly 150 years since a Black man has represented Deep South and deep red Mississippi in the U.S. Senate.
That changed Wednesday evening as Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump. For many in the state and for Black Americans across the nation, Colom's victory reflects the ambitions that were thwarted by generations of systemic oppression and violence.
Janice Johnson, who lives in Greenville in the Mississippi Delta, says having a Black senator has been a long time coming. “In the last few years we have seen great strides,” she said.
Out of all the southern states, Mississippi has a special place in the struggle over Black Americans’ exclusion from the nation’s promises of freedom and justice. There's Ida B. Wells-Barnett, the Mississippi-born journalist who investigated 19th century lynching across the South, and Emmett Till, the 14-year-old whose 1955 kidnapping and murder by white men in Mississippi reinvigorated the Civil Rights Movement.
There's Medgar Evers, the NAACP's first Mississippi field secretary who organized Black voter registration until his 1963 assassination, and Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights leader who challenged Mississippi's all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, who represents Mississippi’s 2nd District, was a student organizer for Hamer while studying at Tougaloo College, where Colom’s victory celebration was held Wednesday night. And now, Thompson is watching his mentee, Sen.-elect Colom, fill a more than 145-year gap of Black leadership in statewide office.
“From my perspective, I now have a partner in Washington,” Thompson said before introducing Colom.
"I can't help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans Day," Colom said during a victory speech. “A moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, when they wouldn't let him vote. But he had the faith that Mississippi could make progress. ... He had faith that a day like this was possible.”
He added, “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.”
Johnson, who watched part of Colom's victory speech from home, says she understands that Black voters, alone, aren't responsible for Colom's win. White voters, too, had to be fed up with the state's economy, school systems and crumbling health care infrastructure for the poor — Black and white — under Republican rule.
“The most important part is we've got to have faith that Mississippi is ready to do the right thing,” an elated Johnson told The Associated Press on Thursday. “We as a people — and Mississippi as whole — are ready to show the nation. We have to work together, and that was his message. He wants to help pull us together.”
Jerome Dunn, a barber in Jackson, echoed Johnson's sentiment.
“It takes everybody to vote, not one single race,” said Dunn, 59, who is Black and also voted for Colom. “I think people are looking for him to work for everybody. People are tired of Republicans and what they believe."
Two came before Colom
Blanche K. Bruce, a Republican, was the second Black man in the Senate from Mississippi after that state's legislature elected him to a six-year term. He served from 1875 to 1881. Hiram Revels, another Republican, was the first after the Senate voted to seat him in 1870 to fill a vacancy left empty since the start of the Civil War. Revels' term expired about a year later.
Bruce and Revels were among 16 Black men from southern states who served in Congress during the period of Reconstruction, which aimed to address the inequities experienced by Black people during enslavement, while preparing reentry for the 11 Southern states that seceded from the union at the start of the U.S. Civil War.
Once Reconstruction ended and federal troops were withdrawn, freed slaves in the South lost many of the freedoms gained following the war as Southern states enforced racial segregation through Jim Crow-era laws.
White conservatives have dominated Mississippi’s Statehouse and congressional delegation ever since. Nearly all were white Democrats as laws restricted where Black people could live, work and go to school. That weight carried on through the Civil Rights era, but during the late 1960s white elected leaders in Mississippi switched political parties and became Republicans.
Colom's win represents “a pretty significant change in Mississippi politics," said Brian Shoup, head of political science and public administration at Mississippi State University.
“We haven't seen a Democrat win the Senate since the 1980s and even then that was a traditional kind of more southern conservative Democrat,” the professor said. “We haven't had an African American senator since the era of Reconstruction, so this is obviously a very significant and important election in Mississippi history.”
Mississippi has been burdened by its racial legacy
Black voters in Mississippi and across the South were faced with the reality of redistricting efforts designed to reduce Black representation in elected positions, set off in late April by a Supreme Court decision that gutted the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965. The ruling helped fuel increased voter turnout.
But it's difficult for many to ignore Mississippi's troubling past involving race relations, from the lynching of Black people by the Ku Klux Klan and other mobs to the killings of Evers and Till.
In his 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, civil rights icon the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. referred to Mississippi as a state “sweltering with the heat of injustice, sweltering with the heat of oppression.”
Colom’s election is historic and means things are changing in parts of the South, said Elnora Fisher, 68, of Greenville, who was born and raised in Mississippi where she remembers that simply living often didn’t seem fair to Black people.
“As I understood, my grandparents always tried to save up to vote," Fisher said. “They had to pay a tax to vote.”
As a child during the 1960s, Fisher said her mother took her to an NAACP meeting. “While we were there the white police stopped the meeting and made us leave,” she said.
Black people in Mississippi should be ecstatic with Colom as a U.S. senator, Fisher added.
“Here in Mississippi, so much has been taken from the poor people and given to the rich people,” she said. “I hope Colom will give back to the people who helped get him where he is.”
Good may come of it all with so many eyes on the results of the contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith, said Shoup, the professor. Mississippians, along with the rest of the nation, may be ready to begin healing from the past.
“This race, the fact that it has been so close, and it has activated so much turnout, might portend the prospects of maybe being able to talk about these things in a more civil and open fashion,” he said.
Sophie Bates in Jackson, Miss., and Aaron Morrison in New York contributed. Williams is a member of AP's Race & Ethnicity team. He reports from Detroit.

sources.news_title: Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom flips Senate seat
sources.text:
In a historic upset, Democrat Scott Colom won his US Senate race in traditionally conservative Mississippi, networks projected on Wednesday, making him the first African American elected to the chamber from the southern state in more than 140 years.
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, prevailed over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in perhaps the most extraordinary seat flip of an already extraordinary US midterm election, in which Democrats crushed the Republicans to reclaim the majority in both chambers of Congress.
Colom praised Mississippi’s long tradition of Black activism and faith in progress.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
“Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” Colom told the jubilant crowd of his supporters in Jackson on Wednesday night. “God didn’t want us to get it the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”
Colom’s win in the deep South adds sting to the stunning rebuke of US President Donald Trump as voters around the country shunned his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.
The latest win, called Wednesday by US news outlets that included CNN, NBC and CBS, will give Democrats 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with 44 for Republicans and one race — in the state of Alaska — still outstanding.
The midterms result was a personal humiliation for Trump as a Democratic wave swept through the Republican heartland. The Democratic flipping of Congress signals an end to Trump’s stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, probe his administration and thwart his appointments.
The Democrats flipped seven other Senate seats that had been held by Republicans, scoring historic breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine — several of which had not changed hands for decades.
The race in ruby red Mississippi went down to the wire — a surprise for many observers who doubted the scale of the Democratic blue wave riding on mounting anger over Trump’s harsh immigration policy, the war in Iran and rising costs of living.
CNN called it for Colom on Wednesday, eight days after election night, with about 99 percent of the vote in and the Democrat ahead of Hyde-Smith by 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent, a difference of 4,585 votes.

Democrat Scott Colom made history Wednesday night, becoming the first Black U.S. senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction after defeating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.
The Associated Press called the race for Colom on Wednesday, Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day, following a lengthy count of absentee and provisional ballots.
Colom’s victory marks the first time a Democrat has won a Mississippi U.S. Senate seat since 1982. The 43-year-old district attorney also becomes the state’s first Black senator since 1874.
Lafayette County voters also favored Colom, giving him 8,525 votes, compared to 8,325 for Hyde-Smith and 373 for independent candidate Ty Pinkins. Colom carried the county by 200 votes, receiving 49.43% of the vote to Hyde-Smith’s 48.27%. Although Hyde-Smith narrowly led Colom in Election Day voting in Lafayette County, Colom gained ground through in-person absentee, mail-in absentee and affidavit ballots to finish ahead overall.
Speaking to a crowd of supporters gathered at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Colom reflected on a campaign that began with little national support and long odds of defeating an incumbent Republican in a traditionally conservative state.
“For me, this journey started with a prayer. And in Mississippi, our prayers often change the course of history,” Colom told the crowd.
He recalled struggling to attract donors and drawing fewer than 10 people to some of his early town hall meetings, but said he continued believing in the possibility of victory.
“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith,” he said.
He also made a commitment to represent all Mississippians, regardless of how they voted.
“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first, I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated. I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m going to treat your future the way I want my future to be,” he said.

Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat in historic victory
JACKSON — Scott Colom won a long-shot bid to oust Mississippi’s Republican incumbent senator, part of a powerful blue wave that propelled Democratic candidates to victory across the country in the midterm elections, the Associated Press reported.
Colom, a local prosecutor, is the first Democrat that Mississippi has elected to the Senate since 1982 and the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era that followed the Civil War.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.
Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.
"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.
Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.
Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.
"They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said.
"It's not something that I did y'all," he continued. "It's something we did."
"In Mississippi, it's local people that make the difference."
Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.
The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.
"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.
"This is purely the work of, particularly, the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.
"This is a historic election."
Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.
"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."
The last black senator in the state before Colom was Bruce who was chosen by the state legislature. It has taken a century and a half for the state to choose a new one.
Colom strove to engage Republican voters, even going to a Trump rally to speak to people in line outside.
Another key moment was his opponent telling voters to "pick another protein" when asked about surging beef prices, something Colom turned into a viral advert of his own.
The contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.
Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.
Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".
The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.
Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.
The 67-year-old Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

Victory is a shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives
Jackson: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalised on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Hyde-Smith, 67, called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede and released a concession speech online shortly afterward.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society, and he repeated that pledge after his victory.
“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated,” Colom said. “I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be” and “work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging status as a political battleground after other victories from North Carolina and South Carolina to Georgia and Texas.
“Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley said ahead of Colom’s victory speech. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great-grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters, most notably Black voters, “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out” in a state that has seen “some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights.”
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see it as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom produced one of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October to rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited to enter. He introduced himself and asked about their concerns.
Later, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said only nine words in six seconds before stepping away: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticising Trump’s policies - especially the Iran war that drove up gas prices and tariffs that caused headaches for Mississippi farmers - without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington - a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving, powerful senators.
There is some irony in Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a US District Court judge. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist.
Colom told the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
At the lectern Wednesday night, Colom said it was appropriate that the race be called on Veterans Day, as he again paid tribute to Evers.
“He served his country, came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote,” Colom said. “But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress.”
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former US agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of his candidacy but said he cares more about what it means for others.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”

sources.news_title: Scott Colom wins Mississippi U.S. Senate race
sources.text:
Scott Colom wins Mississippi US Senate race
District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. Colom, a district attorney, was declared the winner of a hard-fought battle for the Senate seat, and will be the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)
This story was originally published on Mississippi Today.
Democrat Scott Colom has won a hard-fought U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, breaking Republicans’ dominance of statewide offices, ousting one of the state’s sitting senators for the first time since the 1940s and becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Colom, a district attorney in north Mississippi, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and independent Ty Pinkins. Colom on Wednesday secured a come-from-behind triumph that has stunned pollsters, pundits and forecasters across the nation. Hyde-Smith has held the Senate seat since 2018. Mississippi has elected only Republican senators for the last 40 years.
The Democratic victory is an extraordinary upset in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points two years ago, and where Republicans have long maintained a stranglehold on state government and every statewide elected office.
A source close to the Colom campaign said the Hyde-Smith had called him to concede on Wednesday evening. She did not immediately release a statement of her own.
RESULTS: Mississippi 2026 midterm election results
Democratic leaders see Colom’s victory as a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party’s agenda under Trump, who visited the state in the election’s closing days and pleaded with voters to send Hyde-Smith back to the Senate to help advance his agenda.
The Associated Press called the race with 99% of precincts reporting. Colom led 49.2% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. He led Wednesday night by 4,645 votes.
Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator to join the chamber, with Alaska’s Senate election still too close to call.
The AP called the race for Colom based on uncertified results, and the campaigns have said legal challenges are possible.
Colom’s long-awaited win caps more than a week of the nation waiting on Mississippi’s county election officials processing by hand thousands of affidavit ballots to determine the winner.
Colom, 43, will be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis in 1982. He is also the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875. He is also the first Black person elected to any type of statewide office since Reconstruction.
When asked about possibly becoming the first Black man in more than a century to win a U.S. Senate race in the state, Colom said he only wants to make sure he won’t “be the last.”
“I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said. “That’s my focus.”
Most forecasters rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms, voters left little doubt the elections would be a referendum on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and the president’s unpopular war in Iran.
Colom believed his strategy of tying Hyde-Smith to the high cost of gasoline and consumer prices would be enough to pierce the Republicans’ dominance in the Magnolia State. He began to pick up steam rapidly in the campaign’s closing weeks, receiving endorsements and resources from national Democrats.
Colom traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media.
In one viral ad, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should “pick another protein,” with Colom supporters saying they’d rather pick another senator. Another ad riffed off the Oscar-winning movie “Sinners,” which is set in Mississippi and his final ad before the election featured the home of slain civil rights hero Medgar Evers.
Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally for Hyde-Smith in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the other end of the state for a rally with former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior adviser to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.”
And his strategy worked. Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him.
The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year.
Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coastal county that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP. He also flipped Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas of the state that have become swing areas in recent elections.
In a joint statement, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Colom’s victory was historic and vowed to work with him “to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress.”
“Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian, proud husband and father of two, and District Attorney who has dedicated his life to keeping communities safe,” Schumer and Gillibrand said. “He has never stopped fighting for his neighbors, because Mississippi Matters – and he’ll continue to be a champion for Mississippi in Washington.”
For many pioneering Black officials in Mississippi, Colom’s victory is the culmination of decades of organizing, campaigning and civil rights activism. It’s a moment that many never thought they would see in their lifetimes.
Mike Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, unsuccessfully ran against Hyde-Smith twice.
The former cabinet secretary served as an advisor to Colom, handed over his donor and voter lists to the campaign and hoped his losses “paved the road” for the soon-to-be senator, he told Mississippi Today in an interview.
“There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.”
For Colom’s supporters, his victory brought a sense of poetic justice. Then-President Joe Biden in 2022 nominated Colom to a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi. A bipartisan coalition of Mississippi officials supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith used her home-state “blue slip” privilege to oppose it.
Had Hyde-Smith not blocked Colom’s nomination, he likely would have served on the federal judiciary for the rest of his life and never run for the Senate.
But Colom decided to run and cast her as an out-of-touch politician who doesn’t represent Mississippi’s values. Hyde-Smith’s campaign called him a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling Colom a stooge of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros.
Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in early 2018 by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed longtime Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, who retired about halfway into the six-year term. She won two races against Espy, a special election in late 2018 to fill the end of the term Cochran started and a regular election in 2020, and hoped she would gain a third victory.
Hyde-Smith left little doubt that she hoped to stymie Colom’s future as a judge. But in the end, her decision to block him from the federal judiciary cost her a seat in the Senate.

The Democratic victory is an extraordinary upset in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points two years ago, and where Republicans have long maintained a stranglehold on state government and every statewide elected office.
A source close to the Colom campaign said Hyde-Smith had called him to concede on Wednesday evening. Shortly after that, she released a video conceding the race and thanking her supporters.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Democratic leaders see Colom’s victory as a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party’s agenda under Trump, who visited the state in the election’s closing days and pleaded with voters to send Hyde-Smith back to the Senate to help advance his agenda.
The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, eight days after the election, with 99% of precincts reporting. Colom led 49.2% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. He led Wednesday night by 4,645 votes. The AP called the race for Colom based on uncertified results.
Former President Bill Clinton, who campaigned for Colom in northeast Mississippi in late October, congratulated him Wednesday.
“We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it,” Clinton posted on social media. “Scott, you put your heart and soul into this race because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back. I’m honored to have stood alongside you.”
Republican Gov. Tate Reeves posted his congratulations to the senator-elect, writing on X: “I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids!”
Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator to join the chamber, with Alaska’s Senate election still too close to call.
Colom’s long-awaited win caps more than a week of the nation waiting on Mississippi’s county election officials processing by hand thousands of affidavit ballots to determine the winner.
Colom, 43, will be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis in 1982. He is also the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875. He is also the first Black person elected to any type of statewide office since Reconstruction.
When asked about possibly becoming the first Black man in more than a century to win a U.S. Senate race in the state, Colom said he only wants to make sure he won’t “be the last.”
“I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said. “That’s my focus.”
Most forecasters rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms, voters left little doubt the elections would be a referendum on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and the president’s unpopular war in Iran.
Colom believed his strategy of tying Hyde-Smith to the high cost of gasoline and consumer prices would be enough to pierce the Republicans’ dominance in the Magnolia State. He began to pick up steam rapidly in the campaign’s closing weeks, receiving endorsements and resources from national Democrats.
Colom traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media.
In one viral ad, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should pick another protein. Colom supporters in the ad said they’d rather pick another senator. Another ad riffed off the Oscar-winning movie “Sinners,” which is set in Mississippi and his final ad before the election featured the home of slain civil rights hero Medgar Evers.
Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally for Hyde-Smith in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the Gulf Coast for a rally with former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior adviser to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.”
And his strategy worked. Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him.
The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year.
Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coastal area that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP. He also flipped Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas that have flipped between Republican and Democrat in recent elections.
As Colom’s profile rose and Democratic enthusiasm spiked, Hyde-Smith struggled to keep up. She refused to debate Colom or hold open town-hall forums for constituents. She rarely spoke to reporters for longer than a few minutes, often with great hesitation. In the U.S. Capitol, Hyde-Smith avoids hallway interviews that are customary for most members of Congress, and that standoffishness produced awkward encounters that gave Colom ammunition.
Democratic-aligned super PACs, such as American Bridge 21st Century, saw an opportunity and injected millions of dollars into the race, claiming Hyde-Smith is “one of the most hated GOP senators in Congress.”
In a joint statement, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Colom’s victory was historic and vowed to work with him “to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress.”
“Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian, proud husband and father of two, and District Attorney who has dedicated his life to keeping communities safe,” Schumer and Gillibrand said. “He has never stopped fighting for his neighbors, because Mississippi Matters – and he’ll continue to be a champion for Mississippi in Washington.”
For many pioneering Black officials in Mississippi, Colom’s victory is the culmination of decades of organizing, campaigning and civil rights activism. It’s a moment that many never thought they would see in their lifetimes.
Mike Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, unsuccessfully ran against Hyde-Smith twice.
The former cabinet secretary served as an adviser to Colom, handed over his donor and voter lists to the campaign and hoped his losses “paved the road” for the soon-to-be senator, he told Mississippi Today in an interview.
“There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.”
For Colom’s supporters, his victory brought a sense of poetic justice. Then-President Joe Biden in 2022 nominated Colom to a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi. A bipartisan coalition of Mississippi officials supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith used her home-state “blue slip” privilege to oppose it.
Had Hyde-Smith not blocked Colom’s nomination, he likely would have served on the federal judiciary for the rest of his life and never run for the Senate.
But Colom decided to run and cast her as an out-of-touch politician who doesn’t represent Mississippi’s values. Hyde-Smith’s campaign called him a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling Colom a stooge of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros.
Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in early 2018 by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed longtime Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, who retired about halfway into the six-year term. She won two races against Espy, a special election in late 2018 to fill the end of the term Cochran started and a regular election in 2020, and hoped she would gain a third victory against Colom.
Hyde-Smith left little doubt that she hoped to stymie Colom’s future as a judge. But in the end, her decision to block him from the federal judiciary cost her a seat in the Senate.

A Senator Who Once Joked About a 'Public Hanging' Just Lost to Mississippi's First Black Senator in 145 Years
Democrat Scott Colom unseated Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 4,600 votes, becoming the first Black senator directly elected since the Reconstruction era
Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Mississippi Republican who once said she would sit 'on the front row' at a 'public hanging', has lost her Senate seat to Democrat Scott Colom.
Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era, and the first Black senator the state's voters have ever elected directly.
The Associated Press called the race for Colom on Wednesday based on unofficial results, a little over a week after Election Day, Roll Call reported.
Colom won 49.2 per cent of the vote to Hyde-Smith's 48.7 per cent, a margin of just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast. Independent Ty Pinkins took 2 per cent.
Colom celebrated on social media, writing: 'I'll work every day in the US Senate.' He pledged to build a future Mississippians can be proud to call home.
State's Voters Elected Colom Directly
Roll Call's report carried no statement from Hyde-Smith. As absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom said the senator had 'no path to victory'.
Earlier this year, the senator drew criticism when, asked about rising beef prices, she said people had 'so many proteins to choose from', Roll Call noted. Colom turned the line into a viral ad in which a man replies: 'I'd rather pick another senator instead.'
Colom has served as district attorney for four counties in north-east Mississippi since 2016. In 2022, Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked the nomination by withholding her approval.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he had spent years recruiting Colom, telling him: 'You got to run.' Donald Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on 26 October, but it was not enough.
History in Mississippi
Colom is the third Black man to represent Mississippi in the Senate. The first two, Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce, served during Reconstruction and were chosen by the state Legislature rather than by voters.
Bruce left office in 1881, meaning Mississippi has gone 145 years without a Black senator.
The result carries extra weight in a state with a long history of racial violence. Mississippi recorded more lynchings than any other state between 1882 and 1968, according to NAACP figures cited by NPR.
The 'Public Hanging' Remark
Hyde-Smith made her most notorious remark during her 2018 campaign. Praising a cattle rancher who supported her at a campaign stop in Tupelo on 2 November that year, she said: 'If he invited me to a public hanging, I'd be on the front row.'
The video went viral days later, just before her runoff against Democrat Mike Espy, who is Black. Hyde-Smith called the comment an 'exaggerated expression of regard' and insisted that 'any attempt to turn this into a negative connotation is ridiculous'.
Espy's campaign called the remarks 'reprehensible', saying her words showed she 'lacks the understanding and judgment to represent the people of our state'. Hyde-Smith won the 2018 runoff and was re-elected to a full six-year term in 2020.
Her defeat is part of a Democratic wave. The party flipped eight Senate seats to win control, giving the Democratic caucus at least 55 seats and its largest majority since 2011, Roll Call reported. That could grow further in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that remains uncalled.

|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
The last Black man to represent Mississippi in the Senate was born into slavery and left office in 1881.
More than a century later, on Wednesday, Scott Colom, a Democrat, defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., according to The Associated Press, delivering a remarkable upset and becoming the first Black person to be elected to the Senate in his state since the Reconstruction era. Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted to social media on Wednesday evening.
Colom’s victory, which came by a slim margin after more than a week of ballot tallying following the Nov. 3 election, puts an exclamation point on sweeping Democratic victories across the country during this year’s midterms.
For Republicans, the outcome was a jarring rebuke in a reliably conservative stronghold.
Colom’s victory was powered by a diverse coalition that included Black voters angered by policies that targeted their communities and their voting power; white voters frustrated with high prices and the Trump administration’s agenda; and some Republicans dissatisfied by Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to the president and his policies.
For much of this year, Hyde-Smith had been heavily favored to defeat Colom, a district attorney, and win a second term. President Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans have long dominated statewide elections.
But the race appeared to tighten toward the end. Colom, who barreled across the state to homecoming celebrations, city halls and college campuses, worked to introduce himself and capitalize on frustration with Trump and his Republican allies.
The contest attracted national attention in its final stretch. Trump campaigned for Hyde-Smith in the state days before the election, while former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for Colom.
As Democrats racked up win after win, taking back control of the House and Senate in last week’s election, the contest in Mississippi remained unsettled. Colom held a razor-thin lead as lawyers from both parties scrutinized the counting of mail votes as well as affidavit ballots, which are similar to provisional ballots in other states, cast by voters who were listed as inactive or did not bring proper identification.
As the cohort of newly elected senators headed to Washington for orientation, Colom waited in Mississippi for the results. It was fitting, he said, to spend time in the state as his supporters grew hopeful that he would emerge the winner.
During the campaign, Colom emphasized healthcare and lowering costs, among other issues. He did not often dwell on the historic implications of his candidacy.
Mississippi was the first state to send a Black person to Congress, Hiram Revels, who joined the Senate in 1870. He was followed by Blanche Bruce in 1875, who was born in slavery in 1841. Bruce was replaced by a white former Confederate soldier who disavowed the ideals of racial equality and ushered in segregationist policies.
Colom will be sworn into office in January, 146 years after Bruce left office. And because both Revels and Bruce were chosen by state lawmakers, Colom is the first Black senator in the state’s history to be chosen with the people’s votes.
Colom’s victory came three years after Hyde-Smith denied him a chance at a seat on the federal judicial bench by blocking his nomination by President Joe Biden.
He announced his campaign to challenge her in September 2025, criticizing her reluctance to hold public town halls, as well as her unwavering support for Trump.
His record as a prosecutor in northern Mississippi helped insulate him from attacks that he was too liberal for the state. Colom also hammered Hyde-Smith on her votes to cut healthcare and nutritional benefits, a potent message in one of the nation’s poorest states.
And he created a viral campaign ad around her suggestion that voters contending with rising beef prices should “pick another protein,” encouraging Mississippi to “pick another senator instead.”
After the Supreme Court’s decision this year to weaken the Voting Rights Act of 1965, he tapped into backlash among Black voters angered by attempts to dilute their voting power.

sources.text:
His margin of fewer than 5,000 votes caps a midterm wave that has handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, becoming the first Black senator elected from the southern US state in more than 140 years, US networks projected on Wednesday.
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. It was perhaps the most remarkable seat flip of a midterm election in which Democrats won back the majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
CNN, NBC and CBS called the race on Wednesday, eight days after election night. With about 99 per cent of the vote counted, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 49.2 per cent to 48.7 per cent, a margin of 4,585 votes.
“Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” Colom told a jubilant crowd of supporters in Jackson, the state capital, on Wednesday night. “God didn’t want us to get it the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”
In a prayerful, solemn speech, he paid tribute to Mississippi’s long tradition of Black activism and faith in progress.
He will also be the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years.
Hyde-Smith, 67, who has held the seat since 2018, conceded in a video posted on X.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
A blow for Trump
The result in one of the most solidly Republican states deepens the setback for US President Donald Trump. Voters across the country turned away from his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.
Democrats will now hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate and Republicans 44. One race, in Alaska, has yet to be called.
Including Mississippi, Democrats flipped eight Republican-held Senate seats, with breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. Several of those seats had not changed hands for decades.
Control of both chambers of Congress gives Democrats the power to block legislation, investigate the administration and stop Trump’s appointments. The defeat also leaves the 80-year-old president as a lame duck for the final two years of his term.
The race went down to the wire, surprising many observers who had doubted how far the Democratic wave would reach. The wave was driven by mounting anger over Trump’s hardline immigration policy, the war in Iran and the rising cost of living.
“Blue Mississippi is here,” Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate, wrote on X after the projections came in.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him.”
‘The power of prayer’
The first Black senator ever elected in the United States, Hiram Revels, was from Mississippi. He served during the Reconstruction era that followed the American Civil War.
In his speech, Colom described how Revels, a minister by training, used his powerful oratory to win the backing of other politicians for his run for the Senate.
“That’s an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times,” Colom said.
“It’s local people that have faith that Mississippi can make progress, and it’s local people like the people out here who had faith that we could win this election,” he added.

Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom’s Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
sources.text:
Guests
- Angela Lewispsychiatric nurse in Mississippi and daughter of slain civil rights activist James Chaney.
- David Goodmanbrother of slain civil rights activist Andrew Goodman.
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset.
“I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney.
“The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”
Transcript
AMY GOODMAN: We go now to Meridian, Mississippi, where we’re joined by Angela Lewis, the daughter of civil rights activist James Chaney. She was born just 10 days before he was killed by the Ku Klux Klan along with Mickey Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. The date, June 21st, 1964. They were killed by local white supremacists in Mississippi and buried in an earthen dam, not found until 44 days later. The three had traveled to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters.
Angela Lewis, thanks so much for being with us. I’m wondering your thoughts today. And as you watched Scott Colom last night accept the vote as the next Democratic senator from Mississippi, the first time a Black senator will represent Mississippi since Reconstruction, your thoughts?
ANGELA LEWIS: Good morning, and thank you for having me today.
First, I would like to say congratulations to Mr. Scott Colom, his family, and to all of those newly elected officials. I’m very happy, and I just think that this is a day of celebration, not only for Mississippi and for those that won, but I believe that the ancestors are proud and that the work that has been done to get us to this point, it has paid off, and it’s paying off today.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Angela Lewis, if you could talk about some of that work? Leon Russell, the chairman of the NAACP board, said, “This is purely the work of particularly the Black community. There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organizing.” Angela?
ANGELA LEWIS: Yes, the foot soldiers, the boots on the ground, and those that were making the phone calls and doing the work, those are the people, the unsung heroes, that deserve a lot of credit for the wins.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And Mississippi, as we mentioned earlier, has voted for a Republican presidential candidate in every election since the 1980s, and just in 2024, two years ago, Trump won the state by 23 points. So, what do you think accounts for this shift?
ANGELA LEWIS: I think it’s the dedication of the people that stay hopeful and believe that change is possible. And I believe that that’s what we have seen in these recent elections and a lot of the flips and turnovers that we’re seeing. It’s just dedicated people, teachers and the people in the community that’s getting out and registering and getting information out.
AMY GOODMAN: I also wanted to get your response to the county that’s named after the first Ku Klux Klan grand wizard, Nathan Bedford Forrest, Forrest County. Colom won. He also won the county named after Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy. Colom won with 70% of the vote. The significance of this?
ANGELA LEWIS: It’s very significant. But I just believe that people were not voting for a particular color, a particular party. I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed.
AMY GOODMAN: And I also wanted to ask you about the vote that you took. You’re a psychiatric nurse. You’re speaking to us from work. You voted in Meridian, Mississippi. What did you do when you got back in your car? What did you tell your kids?
ANGELA LEWIS: Well, actually, on voting day, I had gotten off from work, and I went to cast my vote. And I sat in my car for a minute and prayed, and I thanked my dad and all of those that worked to make it possible for me to even be able to cast my vote. And when I did cast my vote and I came back to my vehicle, I just had to take a moment again to realize the significance of what could happen in this state and to again just be grateful for those that worked that we would have the opportunity and the privilege to even be able to cast a vote.
AMY GOODMAN: And I also wanted to get your response — I mean, you were cited by Scott Colom, your father, James Chaney. The famous wanted FBI poster — or, it said not “wanted,” but “missing.” James Chaney, your dad, Andrew Goodman and Mickey Schwerner, Michael Schwerner, killed in 1964 when they’d gone to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters. They were first arrested, held in a jail, looked like there was law enforcement involvement when they were followed and then killed and buried in an earthen dam. You had just been born. Your thoughts about your father fighting for African Americans to be able to vote, what he would be feeling this day, James Chaney?
ANGELA LEWIS: I think that he would be, just like the rest of us here in Mississippi, very proud. And I just believe that the day after the Tuesday, after we voted, I believe that next Wednesday, if not the same day, my dad would have gotten up and continued to work and to educate and to register people to vote.
AMY GOODMAN: Well, I want to bring in a person you know well, Angela Lewis, David Goodman. He is the brother of Andrew Goodman, who also, along with your dad and Michael Schwerner, were killed in June. It took 44 days for their bodies to be found, dug up in an earthen dam. The call to the White House — it was Lyndon Johnson, the president at the time — was taken by none other than the late, great journalist Bill Moyers, who was working for Johnson.
David Goodman, thanks so much for being with us. I spoke to you last night just as Scott Colom was about to speak. Your thoughts as you’re on this broadcast, as you’re on Democracy Now! with Angela Lewis today?
DAVID GOODMAN: Well, Amy, it’s — thank you for having us on the show. Hello, Angela. It’s always good to be with you in the spirit world that we live in.
My feelings are that we use words often that — like a “blue wave.” If the Republicans won, it would have been a “red wave.” We’re using the word “tsunami” now. This is not a tsunami. A tsunami is a destruction for all. This is a spiritual change of heart, and it wasn’t easy and a long time coming. And the people of Mississippi have spoken, but the people of the United States are benefiting, whether you’re a Republican or Democrat. And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America. And —
AMY GOODMAN: David —
DAVID GOODMAN: — [Senator]-elect Scott has taught us that.
AMY GOODMAN: David, you never stopped carrying on your brother’s work, Schwerner, Chaney and Goodman’s work, involved with supporting voter registration on colleges throughout the South. Is that right?
DAVID GOODMAN: Yes.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And, David, you referred just now to a spiritual change of heart. How do you think this change of heart came about?
DAVID GOODMAN: You know, we’re a big country. We’re the third or fourth most populous country in the world, and one of the biggest. There’s 340 million of us, so making a generalization is tough. But there’s a lot of pain in our country. And I travel. I’ve been in every state. I’ve lived in many states. I’m in contact with people all over our exquisite and beautiful country. We’re complicated folks. We’re not a homogeneous race or identity group. We’re diverse. And we get fit into these little boxes: You’re Christian, you’re Jewish, you’re Muslim, this, that and the other. And it’s easy for power-hungry, authoritarian people to come in and drive wedges in between us. And this has caused massive problems. And we got hoodwinked by a con artist who’s in the White House using those wedges to make us fight with each other. And I think the American people are sick and tired of it. I am.
And the vote, look, these were just stunning messages. And the authoritarian force, which is heard all over the world, is doubling down. So, we’re not — we can’t stop. We can’t say, “Oh, we won an election. Let’s take a nap and go on vacation.” It’s going to go on indefinitely if we don’t continuously object to authoritarian small group of people running things. And that’s not what happened. I mean, I can’t make — you can’t make this story up. It’s just stunning. You have a person who’s the attorney general of one of our largest states, Texas, who was impeached by his own party and is running. The governor —
AMY GOODMAN: But, of course, he lost. James Talarico beat him, and there was —
DAVID GOODMAN: He did.
AMY GOODMAN: — to say the least, a blue wave in Texas. David and Angela, we do have to go, but I want to thank you both for being with us. David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney. Andrew Goodman, James Chaney and Mickey Schwerner were three civil rights activists who went to Mississippi to register Black people to vote. They were killed June 21st, 1964, cited by Scott Colom last night in his victory address at Tougaloo College, the historically Black college. Tomorrow, we’ll look at the legacy of Medgar Evers, also killed by the Klan, also cited by Scott Colom as the legacy on which he now will rebuild his state.
Coming up, David Sirota of The Lever. Stay with us.
[break]
AMY GOODMAN: “Nunca Más (Never Again)” by La Santa Cecilia in our Democracy Now! studio.
