sources.text:
Democratic challenger Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi election for the US Senate, media projected on Wednesday, making him the Southern state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era that followed the US Civil War.
The result was a stunning upset in the heavily Republican state and expanded on the national drubbing the Democrats delivered to President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections. It was also a historic victory for African Americans in a former slave state that was a hotbed of repression during the civil rights movement of the 1960s.
Democrats strengthen Senate majority
The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member Senate, with the winner in one Senate race from last week’s election — in Alaska — yet to be determined. The Democrats have also gained 41 seats in the House of Representatives so far, holding an advantage of 254 to 168 with 13 races yet to be called.
Republicans lost control of both chambers, leaving Trump facing a Democratic-controlled Congress for the first time in either of his two terms and presenting the opposition party with a chance to block highly partisan legislation and investigate Trump’s administration.
The Mississippi Senate race was one of the final races to be called after the elections.
The latest media-tabulated results showed Colom ahead by 0.5 percentage point, or some 4,600 votes.
Addressing a gathering of supporters who celebrated his victory with “Senator-Elect Colom” signs, Colom said there were times his long-shot campaign felt defeated but “I had to have faith.”
“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone,” Colom said. “They did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith.”
“There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith, and that is another tradition of our state,” he said.
Colom defies expectations
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, became the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.
He harnessed frustration over the cost of living with a breakout campaign ad in which voters ridiculed Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that consumers had multiple proteins to choose from instead of paying rising prices for beef. Colom’s ad rephrased Hyde-Smith’s comment with voters saying, “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
Colom told Reuters in an October interview that Mississippi voters felt betrayed by Trump policies such as the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.
His campaign received a boost from October rallies with two other Black Democratic senators, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey.
Hyde-Smith concedes defeat
Hyde-Smith, 67, who was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and won a special election later that year, had consistently led opinion polls in a state that Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Hyde-Smith near the end of the race.
She congratulated Colom and wished him well in a video posted on social media.
The Democratic victory in Mississippi was a part of a national trend of Democrats finding success in states long dominated by Republicans, including Texas.
With a majority of white voters, Mississippi, deep in the once-segregated South, turned solidly Republican with the political realignment that followed the civil rights movement of the 1960s. Many of the movement’s defining battles took place in Mississippi, where Black people faced discrimination in voting, employment, education and public accommodations.
The last Black candidate elected to the Senate in Mississippi was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.

Scott Colom has won the closely contested Mississippi Senate race, ousting Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, in a major victory for Democrats in the ruby-red US state.

Former Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama have congratulated Colom, whom President Donald Trump called a "shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate" at a campaign rally in Corinth.

Colom wrote to Hyde-Smith, addressing her grievances against him, but the nomination eventually stalled and was officially returned to the White House in January 2024.
Hyde-Smith prematurely claimed victory during an election night speech, saying, "I blocked Scott Colom from being a judge, and you (supporters) blocked him from being a senator."
With Colom's historic triumph, the Democratic Party will have 55 seats when the Senate reconvenes in January, after flipping 8 seats in the midterms.
The Democrats, however, could gain one more seat as the Senate race in Alaska remains uncalled. As of late on 11 November, Mary Peltola led Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan by 3,900 votes.

Colom said that his commitment to all Mississippians was, “I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated. I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m going to treat your future the way I want my future to be.”
He spoke of Mississippi’s history of Black leaders, including Hiram Revels, the first Black senator in the United States, also from Mississippi, who took office in 1870; he spoke of his faith; and he spoke of the difficulty of his campaign, noting that at his first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi, “less than 10 people showed up, but I kept the faith.”
He connected the faith that brought him through the past 23 months with Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, and the other “veterans of the civil rights movement” who were there for his speech at Tougaloo College, an HBCU in Jackson.
It was a reminder that we are always a part of our history — but that at some moments it is more clearly so than in others.
Colom’s was not just any victory, and it was not an easy victory. It was not an expected victory for the Democrats, but Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator in Washington next year (with Democrat Mary Peltola also ahead in the final uncalled Senate race, in Alaska).

"It’s not something I did, it’s something that we did,” Colom said. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this. I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we could show the country that Mississippi matters.”
It was a breath of fresh air after the past decade of the Donald Trump show.
It was, after all, more than a decade ago when Trump, seeking the presidency for the first time, declared, “I alone can fix it.”

sources.news_title: How spectacular Republican own goals helped Mississippi make history
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom was humble in claiming victory late Wednesday night, seizing an eighth Senate seat from the Republicans, this one in the heart of the red south.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he said. “In the Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.”
Colom had not just changed history, he had defied it.
Mississippi has a 36 per cent Black population, more than any other state. But the last time it had a Democratic senator, he was an ardent segregationist first elected in 1947 who Atlantic magazine once described as “one of twentieth century America’s most admired white supremacists”.
The last time Mississippi had a Black senator, he was the son of a slave mother and a white planter, born 20 years before the start of the American Civil War. That man, Republican Blanche Bruce, spoke in the Senate against the “flagrant wrongs” that persisted in Mississippi, where Democrats co-ordinated efforts to suppress the Black vote.
More than 150 years later, the names of the parties have changed. But some of the tactics look familiar. Colom’s win represents a spectacular own goal for Republicans, who have long used controversial tactics to keep the state in their – white -hands. This time, they overreached.
‘All I did was have the courage’
Associated Press called the result for Colom, a 43 year-old former prosecutor and judge, on Wednesday night, more than a week after the election. AP put him ahead by 4669 votes, or 0.5 per cent of the 962,237 counted.
Jubliant supporters gathered in Jackson, Mississippi, one of the most high-profile battlegrounds of the civil rights movement, where Black activists fought – and some died – for democracy.
The victory rally was held on the lawn outside Woodworth Chapel, a meeting ground for prominent civil rights leaders in the 1960s and 1970s, including Martin Luther King, Jr.
“There were many times where I had to have faith,” Colom told supporters. “There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith.
“There were times when I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi… Less than ten people showed up. But I kept the faith.”
All year, Colom has insisted he could win the seat.
“But every time I said it, I pointed out that people were going to give me too much credit for it,” he said. “Because it’s not something that I did, y’all. It’s something that we did.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.”
There is no recount law in Mississippi. The defeated Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, conceded on social media on Wednesday saying: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.”
In a twist of fate, the Republican beaten by Colom could have given him a different career.
In 2022, Colom was nominated by President Joe Biden to be a district court judge.
But Hyde-Smith used her Senate powers to personally prevent the appointment. On election night, when she thought she had won, she even boasted to supporters: “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge and you blocked him from being a U.S senator.”
Hyde-Smith said her team had worked to ensure every legal vote was counted, and it was a “fair and transparent” election.
‘Barriers for voters of colour’
In the era of overt racial segregation in America’s south, the “colour line” was used to refer to the physical and bureaucratic barriers that stood in the way of Black people.
Officials would use tactics like hiding voter registration books from Black would-be voters, and hold white-only primaries.
Modern tactics are marginally less overt.
A Jim Crow era provision still imposes a lifetime voting ban for certain felony convictions, affecting nearly 70,000 people. In August, the Campaign Legal Center said a Republican-led mass closure of polling places particularly disadvantaged voters of colour and low-income voters. It followed a 2013 Supreme Court decision gutting protections against discriminatory voting laws.
“Many Southern localities have taken full advantage of this freedom from federal oversight to impose hard-to-spot practices that create barriers for voters of color in every election,” the CLC found.
Then, in April, the Supreme Court made a decision some dubbed “the worst ruling in a century” and “judicial vandalism“.
In Louisiana v Callais, the six Republican-appointed justices removed what was left of federal protections for minority voters, giving a green light to states to gerrymander districts on racial grounds. Across the country, encouraged by Donald Trump, Republican-majority states started redrawing maps to dilute the Black Democrat vote. Mississippi’s governor declared he would call the state legislature back for a special session to apply a new, openly racial gerrymander.
On top of all this, shortly before the election, more than 230,000 voters were designated inactive. It was the result of a mishandled attempt to “clean the rolls”, initiated by a Republican official. And it disproportionately affected young voters, more likely to vote Democrat.
But the efforts may have backfired.
Professor D’Andra Orey of Jackson State University told the Pulitzer Center that the rolls issue, and the redistricting attempts, inspired a surge in Black voter turnout.
“Some people actually really literally thought that they were going to lose their right to vote, which then mobilised them to get out the vote,” he said.
It was not the only issue, but it was a big one, he said.
Derrick Johnson, president of Black voting rights organisation NAACP, said: “In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy.
“The Trump Administration tried every trick in the book to block voters from the polls, but we showed up and showed out, and we voted.”
‘Blue Mississippi’
Hyde-Smith also helped Colom with unforced errors during her campaign – at one point telling consumers worried about the price of beef to “pick another protein”.
But campaign insiders put Colom’s victory mainly down to his relentless campaigning, which put him in a position to pick up high-profile Democrat support and fundraising late in the day, once the seat looked winnable.
This week Colom complained that, for most of the campaign cycle, analysts had assessed his seat as solid Republican, which “made it much more difficult to fundraise and [is] part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long”.
But eventually, support arrived from Kamala Harris, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pete Buttigieg and Bill Clinton, who chose Mississippi for one of his only two public campaign stops. Barack Obama made an ad for him in the final stretch.
After the result was declared, Clinton congratulated Colom on social media, saying: “We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it!”
The Democrats now hold 55 Senate seats to the Republicans’ 44, with just one seat – Alaska -yet to be called.

sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the largest upsets of this year's midterm elections. Hyde-Smith conceded on Wednesday, eight days after the vote, once news organizations projected Colom the winner. He will be the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since 1881 and the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1982.
Hyde-Smith conceded Wednesday evening in a video message posted online, shortly after the race was projected. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said, adding that she wanted to congratulate Colom and wish him well as he takes on the responsibility of representing the state. Senate Republican leader John Thune said he spoke with Hyde-Smith after her projected loss. Colom spoke at a victory rally at Tougaloo College, near Jackson, on Wednesday.
The race was called after election officials in Hinds County, which includes the state capital, Jackson, finished reviewing affidavit ballots, the term Mississippi uses for provisional ballots. Colom led by more than 4,400 votes when the Hinds County count finished and by about 4,700 once the remaining counties reported, or 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent in unofficial results. His margin had been far narrower for most of the count, at about 2,500 votes earlier this week.
The result adds to a Democratic sweep. With Mississippi decided, Democrats have won 55 seats in the Senate, along with a majority in the House. One Senate race remains uncalled, in Alaska, where Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan as counting continues under the state's ranked-choice system.
Colom, 43, is a district attorney in northeastern Mississippi. He was little known outside the state before this year, and few analysts had the race on the competitive radar. Mississippi has voted for the Republican candidate in every presidential election since 1980, Trump carried it by 23 percentage points in 2024, and Hyde-Smith won her last race, in 2020, by about 10 percentage points. She campaigned on her record and on President Donald Trump's support.
The historical weight of the result is considerable. Mississippi sent two Black men to the Senate during Reconstruction, Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce, and none in the 145 years after Bruce left office in 1881. The state has the highest proportion of Black residents in the country, and it retired a state flag that carried a Confederate emblem only in 2020.
Hyde-Smith, a former state senator and state agriculture commissioner, was appointed to the Senate in 2018 after Sen. Thad Cochran resigned. She won a special election that year to complete his term and a full term in 2020, becoming the first woman elected to the Senate from Mississippi.
The eight days between the election and the concession were contentious. Hyde-Smith had not appeared publicly since election night as of Monday. Her campaign said on Friday that it was "not backing down," and on Thursday its lawyers had sent a letter to county election officials demanding the immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots. Colom's lawyers called the request unlawful, arguing it could lead to different treatment of ballots across counties. Colom pressed Hyde-Smith to explain her path to victory.
Affidavit ballots became the center of the dispute because there were more of them than usual. Voters cast them when their names do not appear on the rolls at their polling place, and election officials then decide whether each voter was eligible. The number rose this year after changes to the state's voter-roll maintenance in the months before the election. In Hinds County, officials accepted 817 affidavit ballots and rejected 1,609, and Colom outperformed his overall share of the vote among those that were counted, a pattern reported in other counties as well.
The outcome also bears on a wider argument about the election. On Monday, Trump asked on social media whether the midterms had been "honest" and blamed voting machines and early ballots, without offering evidence. Hyde-Smith did not echo that claim in conceding. Her statement that she respected the voters' decision came from a Republican who had been one of the president's most reliable supporters in the Senate, in a state he carried easily two years ago.
Republicans have offered several explanations for the scale of their losses. Vice President JD Vance has said the party lost because of the war with Iran. Others have pointed to prices, to the president's choice of candidates in contested primaries and to turnout among Democratic voters, which was unusually high for a midterm. In Mississippi, Colom ran against Hyde-Smith's vote for Trump's tax-and-spending law that cut Medicaid funds, her support for tariffs and the war with Iran, and he labeled her "Cindy High Prices," while Republican groups tried to tie him to national Democrats.
For Democrats, a 55-seat majority changes what is possible in the next Congress. It gives the party a cushion on nominations and on budget measures that require only a simple majority, though it leaves them short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster on most legislation and well short of the two-thirds required to convict in an impeachment trial. Democrats flipped seats this cycle in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Mississippi, and Trump carried every one of those states except Maine in 2024.
For Republicans, Mississippi is the clearest sign of how far the losses reached. The party had not seriously defended a Senate seat there in decades. Whether the result reflects a durable shift or the particular conditions of this election, a war, high prices and an unpopular president in his second term, is a question both parties will be studying before the next campaign begins.
Mississippi's counties must still certify their results by Friday, Nov. 13, and the state will then certify the statewide count. Colom is due to be sworn in when the new Congress convenes in January. The Alaska race is expected to be decided after ranked-choice tabulation, which cannot begin before Nov. 18 if no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes.

sources.news_title: Democrat Scott Colom Elected as Mississippi’s First Black Senator Since Post-Civil War Reconstruction
sources.text:
JACKSON, Miss. — Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom’s favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.
Colom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better,” he said.
National Democrats celebrate
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.”
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters, and she arrived early Wednesday to Colom’s victory party.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley said. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.”
“In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy,” Johnson said.
A race Washington viewed as a long shot
Despite Schumer’s support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see Mississippi as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith’s vulnerabilities crystallized.
He produced of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi’s history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom’s behalf in the campaign’s closing weeks.
The path was always there
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”
Barrow reported from Atlanta and Washington.

Trump carried Mississippi by more than 20 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, and Republicans have controlled the state’s U.S. Senate seats for decades.
Hyde-Smith was initially expected to secure reelection.
However, the political environment shifted during the campaign as voters expressed concerns about rising prices, healthcare costs, and the administration’s war with Iran.
Colom concentrated his campaign on economic issues, particularly the cost of living, wages, and access to rural hospitals.
The district attorney also emphasized his experience as a prosecutor, presenting himself as a candidate willing to work across party lines.
His campaign gained national attention in the final weeks before Election Day.
Democratic organizations increased spending in Mississippi, while former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and other prominent Democrats campaigned on Colom’s behalf.
Trump traveled to Mississippi to support Hyde-Smith, urging Republican voters to keep the seat in GOP hands.
Despite those efforts, Colom built enough support across the state to win the closely contested race.
Hyde-Smith’s 8 Years in Washington
Hyde-Smith entered the Senate in 2018 after then-Gov. Phil Bryant appointed her to replace retiring Republican Sen. Thad Cochran.
She subsequently won a special election and secured a full six-year term in 2020.
During her tenure, Hyde-Smith supported Trump’s policy agenda and aligned with Republican leadership on taxation, immigration, and federal spending.
She also served on the Senate Appropriations Committee, where she worked on federal funding priorities affecting Mississippi.
Her campaign emphasized her conservative record and relationships with Republican leaders.
However, Colom challenged her handling of economic issues and argued that Mississippi needed a different approach to representation in Washington.
The race also featured independent candidate Ty Pinkins, who received approximately 2% of the vote.
Hyde-Smith conceded after the race was called, according to the Associated Press.
Democrats Expand Their Senate Majority
The Mississippi result adds to a series of Democratic victories in Republican-held Senate seats.
According to CBS News, Democrats have flipped eight seats previously held by Republicans, including contests in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, and Mississippi.
With Colom’s projected victory, Democrats are positioned to control at least 55 Senate seats in January, while Republicans hold 44.
Alaska’s Senate race remained unresolved at the time of the Mississippi projection.
The expanded majority will give Democrats greater influence over legislation, presidential nominations, and congressional oversight during the final two years of Trump’s term.
However, the party will still face procedural requirements and political disagreements that could complicate major legislative initiatives.
What Happens Next
Mississippi election officials must complete the remaining ballot reviews and certify the results.
The Associated Press projected Colom’s victory based on the available vote totals and the distribution of outstanding ballots.
Although legal challenges remain possible, Colom is expected to take office when the new Congress convenes in January.
His election will end Hyde-Smith’s tenure and mark a major change in Mississippi’s representation in Washington.
For Democrats, the victory adds another seat to their incoming Senate majority.
For Mississippi, it marks the election of a Democratic senator for the first time since 1982 and the return of a Black representative to the U.S. Senate for the first time since Reconstruction.

sources.news_title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction
sources.text:
Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot-counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Mr. Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it yielded immediate echoes around the country. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday (November 11, 2026) in Mr. Colom's favour after local election officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Ms. Hyde-Smith said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
A spokesman for the Senator said she called Mr. Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic Senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Mr. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalised on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Ms. Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a Senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through,” Mr. Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.
Mr. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better,” he said.
National Democrats celebrate along with Colom
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect's triumph, with nods to the South's emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what's possible for Democrats in the South.”
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Mr. Colom days before the election, addressed Mr. Colom on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back. I'm honoured to have stood alongside you.”
A race Washington once viewed as a long shot
Despite Mr. Schumer's support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy well after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.
The son of a one-time Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Mr. Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Ms. Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallised.
Mr. Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Ms. Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Mr. Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd “pick another senator instead.”
When Mr. Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Ms. Hyde-Smith, Mr. Colom walked the line of Mr. Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Mr. Trump called Ms. Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best President in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
“I love that,” Mr. Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. “Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes.”
The appearance tracked Mr. Colom's tactic of criticising Mr. Trump's policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the President or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Ms. Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony in Ms. Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Mr. Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Senator Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Ms. Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Mr. Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.
Mr. Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Ms. Hyde-Smith.
Mr. Colom called on Mississippi's history. The Senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Mr. Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Mr. Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right.”
Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom's bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice-President Kamala Harris campaigned on Mr. Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.
Despite Republicans' domination, the path was always there. With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than those of its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Governor Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Mr. Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority-Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-Governor Phil Bryant first appointed Ms. Hyde-Smith, who was the state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former US agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Mr. Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Mr. Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially the state's youngest residents, than in his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States Senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance.”

sources.news_title: Another GOP defeat: Mississippi elects first Black senator since 1874
sources.text:
More than a week after the U.S. midterm elections delivered sweeping Democratic gains and cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress, Democrat Scott Colom has completed another extraordinary upset, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi. The victory gives Democrats their 55th Senate seat, compared with 44 for Republicans, with only the race in Alaska still unresolved.
The result is particularly striking in Mississippi, one of the most reliably conservative states in the country. Democrats also scored breakthroughs in traditionally Republican territory elsewhere in the midterms, but Colom’s victory carries a distinction of its own: He is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis won reelection in 1982. Colom, 43, defeated Hyde-Smith, 67, who had served in the Senate since 2018. President Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
Colom also becomes Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era following the Civil War. Mississippi sent two Black Republicans to the Senate during Reconstruction: Hiram Revels, who served in 1870 and 1871, and Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery and was elected by the Mississippi Legislature in 1874 before serving a full Senate term from 1875 to 1881.
The historical significance of Colom’s victory is amplified by Mississippi’s subsequent history of racial segregation and Black disenfranchisement under Jim Crow. During Reconstruction, the Ku Klux Klan also emerged as a violent white supremacist organization targeting Black Americans and their political rights. Among the symbolic results this year was Colom’s victory in Forrest County, a traditionally Republican county named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Klan’s first grand wizard.
The Mississippi race remained undecided for more than a week as election officials processed absentee and provisional ballots. Colom finished election night with a lead of just 43 votes, but his advantage steadily expanded as counties completed their counts. The Associated Press called the race after his lead grew to more than 4,600 votes, a margin large enough that the remaining ballots were not expected to change the outcome. Hyde-Smith subsequently conceded.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer celebrated the result on X. “Blue Mississippi is here. Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him,” he wrote. “Scott will make a fantastic Senator for the people of Mississippi, and I can’t wait to welcome him to the Senate.”
The only Senate contest still outstanding is Alaska. Democrats already hold a 55-44 advantage in the incoming 100-member Senate. A victory in Alaska would increase that majority to 56 seats, significant because most legislation subject to a filibuster requires 60 votes to end debate. The closer Democrats move to that threshold, the fewer Republican votes they would need to advance such measures.
The upset forecasters missed and the protein ad behind it
Unlike races in some other Republican strongholds that had attracted attention well before Election Day, Mississippi was not initially expected to become one of the country’s closest Senate contests. There were signs that Hyde-Smith was vulnerable and that voters were frustrated over the cost of living and high fuel prices, but the Cook Political Report rated the race “Solid Republican” until late October before shifting it to “Likely Republican.”
Trump’s commanding 2024 performance reinforced those assumptions. But Colom spent months insisting that the political environment in Mississippi was changing and urging national Democrats to invest more heavily in his campaign. He argued that unusually strong Black turnout, combined with dissatisfaction over prices and the Trump administration, could make the race competitive. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi’s population.
The morning after Election Day, while much of the country was still surprised by the razor-thin result, Colom said his campaign had expected exactly that kind of race. “Unlike all the people across the country that might be surprised, our campaign, our volunteers, the people of Mississippi are not surprised,” he said. His team had prepared lawyers and volunteers across the state to monitor the remaining count.
Colom’s fundraising accelerated late in the campaign, and prominent Democrats including former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Bill Clinton traveled to Mississippi to support him. But much of his campaign remained intensely local, centered on town halls, grassroots organizing and appeals to voters who had traditionally supported Republicans. His central themes were the cost of living, health care and high gasoline and grocery prices.
Hyde-Smith inadvertently provided Colom with one of his most effective campaign messages. Asked in a local television interview about rising beef prices, she responded, “You have so many proteins to choose from.” Colom’s campaign turned the remark into a viral advertisement featuring Mississippi voters reacting incredulously to the suggestion. One man grilling hamburgers told the camera: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
The ad drew millions of views and became shorthand for Colom’s argument that Hyde-Smith was disconnected from the economic pressures facing ordinary residents. He continued the joke on the campaign trail, including appearances involving food trucks offering voters different protein choices.
Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, a father of two and a practicing Christian who made his faith and family history central parts of his campaign. His mother, Dorothy Colom, broke racial barriers when she was elected a chancery court judge, while his father, Wilbur Colom, was a prominent attorney and longtime Republican who worked for Ronald Reagan.
Before running for the Senate, Colom had already made history in Mississippi politics. He served as a judge and prosecutor before winning election in 2015 as district attorney for the state’s 16th Judicial District, becoming the first Black person elected to the post. He built his Senate campaign around the argument that he could attract both the state’s large Black electorate and moderate or traditionally Republican voters.
His victory now places him in a political lineage stretching directly back to Reconstruction. Colom has said the significance of becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator in generations also carries a responsibility to ensure that he is not the last, and that his performance in office should make it easier rather than harder for future candidates from similar backgrounds to succeed.
The election also carries an element of personal political reversal. President Joe Biden nominated Colom in 2022 to become a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith refused to return the Senate Judiciary Committee’s required “blue slip,” preventing it from advancing.
Hyde-Smith later boasted about blocking the nomination. “He thought he was going to be a federal judge, and I blocked him,” she said during her reelection campaign. Colom has denied that his Senate run was motivated by revenge, instead emphasizing affordability, health care and government accountability.
Now, the man Hyde-Smith prevented from reaching the federal bench will replace her in the U.S. Senate. As Colom put it while the ballots were still being counted: “The bottom line is this is the beginning of a new direction for our state.”

sources.news_title: Mississippi electing Scott Colom as senator may be one of the biggest shocks of 2026
sources.text:
First Person - There have been many shocks in American politics the past few weeks, but there's nothing that quite compares to the election of Senator Scott Colom in Mississippi.
Colom, a Democrat and Black district attorney, stunned poll watchers by narrowly defeating the white Republican sitting US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The final vote, which took more than a week to confirm, shows Colom winning by a narrow 4000 or so votes - a result pretty much nobody outside of Mississippi saw coming even in the face of a mighty "blue wave" for Democrats nationwide.
The Associated Press and CNN projected Colom as the winner on Thursday (NZ time).
It is impossible to fully describe the magnitude of a Black Democrat winning a Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that's been deeply Republican for decades and has a long, sordid history of oppression of Black voters.
Colom will be the first Black senator in Mississippi since 1881 - and that man was born enslaved.
He's also the first Democrat elected there since 1982. The campaign of Colom, 43, seemed filled with energy, compared to the lethargic efforts by Hyde-Smith, 67.
Sixty, seventy years ago, he could have been killed for even trying to vote in Mississippi, where the Ku Klux Klan and others fought any attempt by Black people to vote well in the 1960s.
Mississippi is a word which feels haunted, slippery with meaning. There's no more evocative American state name, with all that entails.
The roots of my family run deep there. My mother was raised there, my grandparents and great-grandparents are buried there, in a quiet cemetery beneath the trees, tucked away down shadowy side roads.
I lived there myself from the ages of 18 to 25, from a freshman at the University of Mississippi to a fumbling young working journalist.
In August, I visited friends and family in Mississippi for the first time in years. The political campaign signs were only starting to come out, but nobody was talking about Scott Colom winning the Senate race. It didn't seem possible.
Every place on Earth has a tragic past if you dig far enough, but Mississippi is unique in its stains and glories. I can think of nowhere else I've lived where the absolute worst and the shining best of a place are so deeply intertwined, where one seemingly cannot exist without the other.
The horrors that were visited on the Black population there in the 20th century still turn my stomach, the suppression, cruelty and casual dehumanisation. The story of Emmett Till - a 14-year-old boy tortured and murdered by white racists in 1955 for allegedly daring to whistle at a white woman - is as good as any to illustrate how horrible things could get.
My mother was just about the same age as Till and grew up an hour or two away from where his blood was spilled. But she knew nothing about it at the time, until many years later when the story began to seep out into the wider culture. The South endlessly romanticises itself, which can create both great stories and cover up hard truths.
A place can have a terrible past and yet still have things to admire and love; in our everything-is-good-or-evil digital world, it can be hard to explain a place that is full of troubles and still working hard to be better, and yet can be full of kindness and talent. Mississippi is complicated.
The Mississippi I visited in August felt like it was inching forward still with reconciling that past - the university campus of what's known as 'Ole Miss' was now dotted with prominent signs about the historic racial outrages and terror, and the looming county courthouse, as Southern as it gets, now also features a large memorial about lynchings held there.
A monument to James Meredith, who became the first Black student at Ole Miss despite bloody, fatal protests in 1962, now stands proudly beside the campus library. Courage, a sign proclaims.
Bad things still happen in Mississippi all the time, like just this past week when two white female university students made global news for racist gestures toward Black students. Yet one hopes those foolish students are the exception of their generation - youth aged 18 to 29 overwhelmingly voted for Colom in Mississippi, by a 30-point margin.
Colom marked his campaign with viral and witty ads (if you haven't heard about "pick another protein", watch it above), but he chose to end his run with a deeply serious ad filmed at the home of Medgar Evers, a civil rights activist shot dead in his driveway in 1963 while his wife and children waited inside.
"It's a powerful reminder of the sacrifice to gain the ballot, and nobody sacrificed more than Medgar Evers and his family," Colom told the media Friday.
"What was important to me about that ad is we didn't ask people to vote for me. We just talked about the sacrifice, talked about the story. We just wanted that to be the closing ad because I wanted that to be the last message that the people of Mississippi heard."
Colom's victory is not a rejection of the past. It's steeped in the past, and hopes for a future that eases Mississippi's massive inequalities.
Mississippi's William Faulkner famously said "The past is never dead. It's not even past," and that's still as Mississippi a thought as you can get.
I lived in Mississippi, loved a lot about it, grimaced at some things, and learned so very much about stories, writing and myself in my time there.
One election win doesn't fix America, of course, and Scott Colom may turn out to be just another politician. But even he can't stop what he symbolises today, in the often troubled country I came from that can still sometimes manage to surprise me.

sources.text:
Mississippi Goes Blue: Democrat Scott Colom Ousts "100% MAGA" Hyde-Smith
Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, NBC News, CNN and the Associated Press projected Wednesday. President Trump carried the state by 23 points in 2024, and the win gives Democrats at least 55 Senate seats next year.
CNN PROJECTS THAT SCOTT COLOM WINS THE SENATE RACE IN MISSISSIPPI! pic.twitter.com/7MVfp94PAh
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 11, 2026
Hyde-Smith called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede, two sources close to his campaign told CNBC.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer posted on X: "Blue Mississippi is here."
Colom is the first Democrat Mississippi has elected to the Senate since 1982, a few weeks before he was born, and he will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction. He is the eighth Democrat to flip a Republican-held Senate seat this year, and no Democrat in the next Senate will represent a redder state.
Election night ended with Colom ahead by 43 votes with more than 95% counted, as we noted the next morning. Affidavit ballots, cast provisionally when a voter's eligibility is in question, then broke his way, as did late returns from Hinds County, home to Jackson, where he took about 80% of the vote. With an estimated 99% counted on Tuesday, he led 49.18% to 48.72%, with independent Ty Pinkins at 2.1%, according to the AP's count as reported by CNBC.
By Wednesday afternoon the AP had Colom ahead by 4,585 votes. His campaign put the margin at 5,568 once official results from 24 counties that had certified were added, and said shortly before the call: "The data is clear: Scott Colom will be the next U.S. Senator for Mississippi and his victory is now a guarantee," the Mississippi Free Press reported.
In a Nov. 6 Facebook statement, Hyde-Smith wrote, "We are not backing down," adding, "This election is not over," and promised that her team would "see this through to the very end!" according to the Free Press. Colom had lawyered up the day after the election ("We got the lawyers who are ready to make sure the law's followed," he said), and Democratic election lawyer Marc Elias said his firm was leading the legal effort on Colom's behalf, the Daily Beast reported. Elias is reportedly under Justice Department investigation in the Peltola case in Alaska, as we noted Tuesday.
Colom hit Hyde-Smith over her vote for Trump's "big, beautiful bill" and its Medicaid cuts. He branded her "Cindy High Prices" over her support for Trump's tariffs and the costly war with Iran. One viral video from his campaign seized on her remark that Mississippians facing high beef prices "have so many proteins to choose from," with voters saying, "Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator."
"We were never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause," Colom told NBC News before the call, saying Hyde-Smith "gave away our voice in the war in Iran," and faulting his own party for not competing in the state.
A majority of Mississippi voters disapproved of Trump's job performance, according to NBC News exit polling, and majorities said his policies, tariffs included, hurt the economy and that military action in Iran was wrong.
Trump endorsed Hyde-Smith more than a year before the midterms, calling her "100% MAGA," and he flew to Mississippi to campaign eight days before the election. Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker and Raphael Warnock campaigned for Colom, and Barack Obama appeared in one of his ads.
Hyde-Smith had blocked Colom's nomination to a federal judgeship during the Biden administration; Colom told NBC News he has since forgiven her. On Monday he blamed the Cook Political Report and other forecasters, which rated his race solidly Republican for much of the cycle, for making it harder to raise money:
At some point, we have to talk about @CookPolitical and other "prognosticators" who had me and other southern candidates labeled as solid R for much of the campaign cycle. They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so...
— Scott Colom (@scott_colom) November 9, 2026
Alaska is now the only Senate race left uncalled, and Democrat Mary Peltola's lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan has grown past every vote cast for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

sources.news_title: Mississippi elects first Democratic senator in 44 years as Dems finally find a winning strategy: Spend nothing and let the other candidate talk beef
sources.text:
For four decades, the typical plan the national Democratic Party had for Mississippi was to leave it alone. Seems like they finally found their winning strategy: Democrat Scott Colom has narrowly eked out a razor-thin win over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, and arguably, it was because he let her do the talking.
Colom is the first Democrat Mississippi sent to the Senate since noted segregationist John Stennis won his last term in 1982. Mississippi, which up until last week’s elections was nearly unanimously rated as a solid Republican state, is the only state in the country that doesn’t allow automatic recounts, meaning the loser has to go to court to get the votes reexamined.
What’s notable about the race is the sheer lack of attention it has garnered (at least, up until recently) and how Colom even became a viable contender in the first place. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom, a district attorney, to the federal bench in northern Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported him. Hyde-Smith blocked the nomination in 2023, citing his “opposition to legislation to protect female athletes” and past support from a PAC funded by George Soros. Had she let it through, Colom might be a federal judge today instead of her successor. Two years later, he announced his campaign against her.
Likely Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer saw an opening. He told the New York Times in 2025 he wanted to help elect a Democrat in Mississippi and find other winning tickets in states that would be relatively cheap to compete in. While he referenced Colom at the time, Colom said Schumer isn’t why he ran: in his launch video, he referenced his two daughters and Hyde-Smith’s vote for a law he said would cut more than 100,000 Mississippians from their health care.
Kitchen table economics
That kitchen table economic sentiment may be why Colom won in a state represented, for now, by a cattle rancher.
In February, a reporter asked Hyde-Smith, who also married a fifth-generation cattle rancher, what Republicans were doing about rising beef prices. “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she said. Ground beef had risen from $5.55 a pound when President Donald Trump returned to office to $6.79 in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Colom’s campaign turned her answer into an ad of Mississippians reacting to it, a move widely regarded to have tipped the scale in his favor. The ad’s release was also when the national Democratic Party started showing up. Former President Bill Clinton rallied for him in Tupelo on Oct. 30. “Scott is the correction,” Clinton told the crowd. Still, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee put just $500,000 into the race in its final week, while Hyde-Smith raised about $6.3 million for her campaign. Colom wasn’t alone, though: counting outside groups, money spent backing him outpaced money backing Hyde-Smith roughly three to one, according to FEC data.
The win was mostly Colom: he held events in all 82 Mississippi counties, the Washington Post reported, while Hyde-Smith hadn’t held a town hall in six years. Local organizers did the rest. When Holmes County, home to about 15,000 people, reported its votes near midnight on election night, its surge in turnout put Colom ahead by 28 votes.
Colom also flipped Forrest County, named for the Ku Klux Klan’s first grand wizard, 12,064 to 9,749, and won Jefferson Davis County, named for the president of the Confederacy, 2,943 to 1,534. He would also be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery and left office in 1881, and the first Black senator the state’s voters have ever chosen directly. Mississippi’s first, Hiram Revels, was also the nation’s first Black senator, appointed by the state legislature in 1870.
Democrats with 56 seats
Democrats entered Election Day with 47 Senate seats and were projected to flip at least seven. Now already with control of both chambers, Colom makes it 55. If Democrat Mary Peltola holds her narrow lead in Alaska, where counting continues, it’s 56.
The difference between 54 and 56 shows up in the filibuster. Most legislation needs 60 votes to end debate and pass the Senate. At 54 seats, Democrats would need six Republicans to cross over, but at 56, they need four.
A bigger majority also gives Schumer room on his own side. With 51 seats, a single Democratic defection can sink a nominee or a party-line vote. With 56, he can lose several and still confirm judges and officials, which takes only a simple majority. That matters for Trump’s picks as well: a Democratic Senate can now block his nominees to the federal bench, the kind of seat Colom was once denied.
The lesson of Mississippi isn’t only for Democrats. Voters named the cost of living and government corruption as their top two issues in AP exit polls. Two years earlier, voters who were worried about the economy broke for Trump by 2 to 1. The issue that won Republicans the White House helped cost them the Senate.
Some Republicans saw it coming. But Trump called affordability “a con job” by Democrats, even as nearly three-quarters of his own voters rated the cost of living bad or the worst ever. Vice President JD Vance warned his party not to blame young people for socialism’s growing appeal when they couldn’t afford homes, then answered one young voter’s affordability question with a joke.
“We used to own the affordability issue just two years ago,” Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York said. “We let that slip away.”

sources.news_title: Democrat seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won his US Senate race in traditionally conservative Mississippi, networks have projected, making him the first African-American elected to the chamber from the southern state in more than 140 years.
Mr Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, prevailed over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in perhaps the most extraordinary seat flip of an already extraordinary US midterm election, in which Democrats crushed the Republicans to reclaim the majority in both chambers of Congress.
Mr Colom's win adds sting to the stunning rebuke of President Donald Trump as voters around the country shunned his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.
The latest win, called yesterday by US news outlets that included CNN, NBC and CBS, will give Democrats 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with 44 for Republicans and one race - in the state of Alaska - still outstanding.
Ms Hyde-Smith, in office since 2018, conceded the race in a video posted to X.
"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," the 67-year-old senator said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."
'Blue Mississippi is here'
The race in ruby red Mississippi went down to the wire - a surprise for many observers who doubted the scale of the Democratic blue wave riding on mounting anger over Mr Trump's harsh immigration policy, the war in Iran and rising costs of living.
CNN called it for Mr Colom, eight days after election night, with about 99% of the vote in and the Democrat ahead of Ms Hyde-Smith by 49.2% to 48.7%, a difference of 4,585 votes.
"Blue Mississippi is here," the US Senate's top Democrat Chuck Schumer proclaimed on X after the projections came in.
"Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him."
Mr Colom is set to become the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years, and first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era after the Civil War.
Mississippi has no law mandating a recount in the event of a tight election. But legal teams from both candidates are reported to be ramping up for potential challenges.

sources.text:
Democrat Colom stuns Mississippi, becomes state's first Black senator since 1874
Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's Senate race. The historic upset strengthens the Democrats' majority and ends a 150-year barrier.
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race, according to media projections, becoming the first Black senator from the Southern state in more than 150 years in a historic upset that further strengthens the Democrats' position after the November 3 midterm elections.
Colom's victory marks the first time since the Reconstruction era following the US Civil War that Mississippi will send a Black representative to the Senate. The last Black candidate elected to the state's Senate seat was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.
The result is particularly significant in a state that has remained a Republican stronghold. President Donald Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election and personally campaigned for Hyde-Smith towards the end of the Senate race.
The Mississippi contest was among the last outstanding races from the November 3 elections to be called. Vote counting continued for more than a week, with the contest remaining extremely close. At one point, Colom was ahead by just a few dozen votes. The latest media-tabulated results put him more than 4,500 votes ahead, a margin of around 0.5 percentage point.
The 43-year-old district attorney also becomes the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.
DEMOCRATS STRENGTHEN POSITION IN SENATE
Colom's win further expands the Democrats' advantage in Congress, following their sweeping gains in the midterm elections, which saw Republicans lose control of both chambers.
The Mississippi result gives Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member Senate, with the outcome of one remaining race in Alaska yet to be determined. In the House of Representatives, Democrats have gained 41 seats so far and hold a 254-168 advantage, with 13 races still awaiting calls.
The loss of both chambers has left Trump facing a Democratic-controlled Congress for the first time during either of his presidential terms. The opposition party will now have greater leverage to block partisan legislation and launch investigations into his administration.
HOW COLOM PULLED OFF THE UPSET
Hyde-Smith, 67, was first elected to the Senate in 2018 and had consistently led Colom in opinion polls in a state that has traditionally favoured Republicans. Trump's campaign appearance in her support had added to her advantage.
However, Colom told Reuters in an October interview that voters in Mississippi felt betrayed by Trump's policies, particularly the war in Iran, which had pushed up fuel prices.
During his campaign, Colom focused on grassroots outreach, holding town halls and visiting public housing communities, festivals and food trucks to connect with voters.
"We did it the hard way, the grassroots way," he told Reuters.
His campaign also received a boost from October rallies featuring Democratic Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey.
The contest also carried a personal political history between the two candidates. In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by then-President Joe Biden to serve as a federal district judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker, had supported his nomination.

WASHINGTON: Democratic challenger Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi election for the US Senate, media projected on Wednesday (Nov 11), making him the Southern state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era that followed the US Civil War.
The result was a stunning upset in the heavily Republican state and expanded on the national drubbing the Democrats delivered to President Donald Trump's Republicans in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member Senate, with the winner in one Senate race from last week's election - in Alaska - yet to be determined. The Democrats have also gained 41 seats in the House of Representatives so far, holding an advantage of 254 to 168 with 13 races yet to be called.
In losing control of both chambers, Trump faces a Democratic-controlled Congress for the first time in either of his two terms, presenting the opposition party a chance to block highly partisan legislation and investigate Trump's administration.
The Mississippi Senate race was one of the final outstanding races to be called since last week's elections. Mississippi election officials have spent more than a week counting ballots in a race that was so tight that Colom at times led by only a few dozen votes. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4,500 votes, or 0.5 percentage points.
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, became the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.
Hyde-Smith, 67, who was first elected in 2018, had consistently led in opinion polls in a state that Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Hyde-Smith near the end of the race.
Colom told Reuters in an October interview that Mississippi voters felt betrayed by Trump policies such as the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.
On the campaign trail, Colom said, he focused on reaching voters through town halls as well as visits to public housing, festivals and food trucks. "We did it the hard way, the grassroots way," he said.
October rallies with Democratic Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey boosted his campaign.
The last Black candidate elected to the Senate in Mississippi was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.
In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a federal district judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.

Mississippi Elects First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
                        Democratic nominee Scott Colom's victory is a seismic shift for the state
                    
|                          By Newser Editors and Wire Services                                                                                                            Posted Nov 11, 2026  5:22 PM CST                                                       | 
Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, the AP reports.
- Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.
The AP called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local election officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist.
- Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on discontent with the economy, Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term, and the large number of Black people in the state. "They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.
- Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society. "It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America—a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it," he said.
- The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family. "In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination, and the three decades it took to win a conviction. "He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right."
