sources.text:
In an unexpected development just days after the election, CNN has declared Democrat Scott Colom the winner of Mississippi’s U.S. Senate contest. This result represents a significant upset in the midterm elections of 2026, where Democrats have achieved historic victories.
The network’s Decision Desk made its announcement in the late afternoon after additional ballots from crucial counties widened Colom’s lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. With about 98.6 to 99 percent of ballots counted, Colom garnered 49.2 percent, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7 percent, yielding a margin of approximately 4,500 to 4,700 votes.
Independent candidate Ty Pinkins contributed 2.1 percent to the total vote count.
The election remained unresolved for several days due to Mississippi’s methods for handling affidavit ballots—provisional ballots that are cast when a voter’s eligibility or ID cannot be verified on Election Day—as well as outstanding absentee ballots. Counties were tasked with processing postmarked mail ballots and addressing ID verification on provisional ballots. With the addition of these ballots, Colom’s slim lead, which fluctuated at a few thousand votes for the majority of the period, steadily increased.
POLL: Will America Regret Giving The Democrats Power?
Scott Colom will defeat Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a major upset to become the first Democrat that voters in deep-red Mississippi have elected to the chamber in more than four decades, CNN projects. https://t.co/LIrSavsJ01 pic.twitter.com/DLvYVX3MNB
— CNN (@CNN) November 11, 2026
CNN’s projection followed updates that included results from Hinds County, a region leaning Democratic, and subsequent counts from other counties.
CNN stood out as the first major news organization to declare Colom the winner, doing so around 5:05 p.m. Eastern time. The Associated Press made their call shortly before 6 p.m. Eastern after updates from Jackson County showing more than 2,100 votes placed Colom ahead by approximately 4,669 votes of over 962,000 total counted. Other prominent election forecasters followed suit soon afterward.
While official certification timelines remain later, with counties needing to finalize results by November 13, and statewide certification due December 3, it is anticipated that the remaining uncounted ballots—estimated to be fewer than 12,000—would not be enough to alter the race’s outcome, based on previous trends.
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from northern Mississippi, will be the first Democrat to secure a Senate seat from the state since John Stennis in 1982 and the first Black individual to hold statewide office in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. Hyde-Smith’s campaign confirmed her concession to Colom on Wednesday evening.
In her last full term won in 2020, Hyde-Smith triumphed by about 10 percentage points, defeating Democrat Mike Espy with 54.1 percent to 44.1 percent, a spread of roughly 130,820 votes from over 1.3 million cast. It had been over four decades since Mississippi elected a Democratic senator, and President Donald Trump carried the state by more than 22 points in the 2024 election.
This outcome elevates the Democratic caucus to 55 seats in the Senate, which will convene in January 2027, pending results from the uncalled Alaska race where Democrat Mary Peltola has claimed victory, currently holding a narrow edge over incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan (R-AK).

sources.news_title: Democrats Flip Deep-Red Mississippi as Hyde-Smith Falls to Colom
sources.text:
JACKSON, Miss. — Senate Republicans have lost reliably red Mississippi.
The Associated Press projected Wednesday that Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, has defeated incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., more than a week after Election Day. The call gives Democrats 55 seats in the U.S. Senate to Republicans' 44, with Alaska still undecided, according to Fox News. CBS News and NBC News also projected Colom the winner.
Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted to X on Wednesday evening. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well, as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state." A source familiar told Fox News Digital that Hyde-Smith had spoken with Colom and conceded the race.
No Democrat had won a Mississippi Senate seat since 1982. Colom will become the state's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, according to The New York Times and NBC News, taking the seat once held by Hiram Revels, the nation's first Black senator, elected in 1870.
What Happened
The race was deadlocked until the final weeks of October, according to Fox News. President Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024 and campaigned in the state for Hyde-Smith days before the election. A seven-figure, last-minute ad buy by the Senate Leadership Fund, a PAC closely tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., was not enough to stop Colom's momentum, Fox News reported.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for Colom, according to The New York Times.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., took a victory lap before the AP called the race. "We will work hand in hand with Scott to fight for Mississippians' health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress and look forward to welcoming him to our caucus," they said, according to Fox News.
Colom addressed his coalition during the campaign, telling voters his party had too long written off the state. "But for too long we were also a betrayed cause by the national party because they did not compete in this state," he said, per NBC News.
Why It Matters
The loss is the eighth Republican-held Senate seat Democrats have flipped this year, according to NBC News. Fox News reported that 55 Democrats will hold Senate seats next year, with one race still pending in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola is in a neck-and-neck contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska.
Exit polling cited by NBC News found a majority of Mississippi voters disapproved of Trump's overall job performance, said his policies including tariffs hurt the economy, and opposed U.S. military action in Iran.
The result lands two years after Trump won the state by 23 points — and after he personally campaigned for Hyde-Smith. Republicans now confront a Senate map that has shrunk to 44 seats with Alaska outstanding.
It is not yet known when Colom will be sworn in or how the final Alaska result will reshape the chamber's margins.
Our Take
Let's be clear about what just happened. Mississippi — a state Trump won by 23 points — just sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 44 years. That is not a fluke. That is a message, and the people delivering it are the same voters Republicans have spent two years assuming would never leave.
Hyde-Smith had the president's endorsement. She had a seven-figure lifeline from the Senate Leadership Fund. She had everything the party establishment could throw at a race — and it wasn't enough. Why? Because when voters are angry about prices, and Washington keeps telling them the economy is fine, they stop listening to the people who tell them that.
Some in the GOP will want to blame the usual suspects — the media, the timing, the turnout. But the exit polling cited by NBC News is brutal: a majority of Mississippi voters disapproved of Trump's job performance. A majority said tariffs hurt the economy. A majority opposed military action in Iran. That is not a turnout problem. That is a message problem.
Colom ran as a district attorney and talked about costs and health care. He didn't run as a socialist. He didn't run on defunding anything. He ran on the kitchen-table issues Republicans used to own — and he won in the reddest state in the country.
If Republicans want to hold the Senate in two years, they need to stop assuming deep-red states are safe and start proving they deserve them. Mississippi just proved the price of taking voters for granted — and it wasn't cheap.

Shock as Democrat wins tight Mississippi senate race
A Democrat has won a stunning upset in Mississippi's US Senate after days of counting.
Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday to become the Southern state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era that followed the Civil War.
The result was a stunning upset in the heavily Republican state and expanded on the national drubbing the Democrats delivered to President Donald Trump's Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.
The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member Senate, with the winner in one Senate race from last week's election — in Alaska — yet to be determined.
The Democrats have also gained 41 seats in the House of Representatives so far, holding an advantage of 254 to 168 with 13 races yet to be called.
In losing control of both chambers, Trump faces a Democratic-controlled Congress for the first time in either of his two terms, presenting the opposition party a chance to block highly partisan legislation and investigate Trump's administration.
The Mississippi Senate race was one of the final outstanding races to be called since last week's elections. Mississippi election officials have spent more than a week counting ballots in a race that was so tight that Colom at times led by only a few dozen votes. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4500 votes, or 0.5 percentage point.
Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, became the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.
Hyde-Smith, 67, who was first elected in 2018, had consistently led in opinion polls in a state that Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Hyde-Smith near the end of the race.
Colom told Reuters in an October interview that Mississippi voters felt betrayed by Trump policies such as the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.
On the campaign trail, Colom said, he focused on reaching voters through town halls as well as visits to public housing, festivals and food trucks.
"We did it the hard way, the grassroots way," he said.
October rallies with Democratic Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey boosted his campaign.
The last Black candidate elected to the Senate in Mississippi was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.
In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a federal district judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.

sources.news_title: Hyde-Smith concedes to Democrat Scott Colom as winner
Democrat Scott Colom becomes Mississippi’s first Black US senator since Civil War Reconstruction
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom becomes Mississippi’s first Black US senator since Civil War Reconstruction
Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith after days of ballot counting, becoming Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
Hyde-Smith posted a concession video on social media, and a spokesman for Hyde-Smith confirmed that she had called Colom to concede.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.
Also Read: Nvidia shares sink 9% amid reports of possible CEO Jensen Huang ouster
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don’t come up with excuses as to why we can’t do it,” he said.
Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer celebrated on social media.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done,” Schumer wrote. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.”
A race Washington once viewed as a longshot
Despite Schumer's support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy well after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.
Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Also Read: Nvidia preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang amid affair probe: Report
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
“I love that,” Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. “Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes.”
The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.
Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi's history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom's bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.
Despite Republicans' domination, the path was always there
With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”

sources.news_title: Democrat Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith to be Mississippi’s first Black senator since 1881
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom’s bid for a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi was dismissed as improbable — a long-shot effort standing up against the weight of political history that has shut Black people out of statewide representation for generations. While Mississippi was the first in the country to send a Black person to the U.S. Senate, the state has not had another Black U.S. Senator since 1881.
But this year of historic firsts made its way to Mississippi on Wednesday, with Decision Desk HQ projecting Colom to win his race against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, flipping another GOP-held seat as Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.
Colom’s victory will cement a historic high of seven Black U.S. senators serving at one time: He and projected Senator-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois will join Sens. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Cory Booker of New Jersey, Tim Scott of South Carolina and Raphael Warnock of Georgia. In total, only nine Black men and five Black women have held a U.S. Senate seat.
Hyde-Smith’s loss, along with the defeat of longtime Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, will bring the number of Republican women in the chamber down from 11 to eight.
As Colom’s campaign picked up steam in the waning weeks before Election Day, President Donald Trump attempted to shore up Hyde-Smith by traveling to a rally in Corinth, Mississippi. Standing next to the president, she spoke only nine words: “Is this not the best president of our lifetime?” Trump then proceeded to talk for the next hour and a half.
That last-minute show of support from the president was not enough to secure a win. It comes at a time when advocates working to increase the number of Republican women in elected office have pointed to structural issues they believe hinder their efforts.
Black candidates face their own set of systemic and racial realities that have historically blocked their ability to advance in politics. Despite having the largest concentration of Black residents of any U.S. state, Mississippi currently has zero Black people in statewide office. The last Black person to hold a U.S. Senate seat in the state was born into slavery. The last time a Democrat won a U.S. Senate race there was in 1982.
Colom is a former prosecutor who has worked as district attorney for the 16th Judicial District of Mississippi since 2016. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as a U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Mississippi, which Hyde-Smith ultimately helped to block by declining to return a “blue slip,” a document used to allow senators from the home state of judicial nominees to signal their support or disapproval.
In her reasoning, she cited Colom’s public support for transgender rights, which included signing a 2021 letter criticizing the criminalization of transgender people and gender-affirming healthcare around the country.
Three years later, Colom has now unseated Hyde-Smith from her position in what may be viewed as one of the biggest comeback moments of the midterms. Much of the messaging throughout his campaign focused on cost of living, low wages and the ways he feels voters in his home state have been overlooked by political leaders. This includes his opponent, Hyde-Smith, who during a February interview suggested that people choose a different protein option in response to the rising cost of beef. It also includes leaders within his party, Colom has said.
National Democrats are “conditioned not to care about Mississippi,” Colom told The Washington Post ahead of Election Day. “To me, you can’t be a party that cares about working people if you don’t care about working rural people in Mississippi who are struggling.”
Part of the struggles Mississippi residents face are barriers to voting access that include a strict photo ID law, no early voting and limited absentee voting, and disenfranchisement for people with certain felony convictions. On Election Day some residents took to social media to report being turned away at polling sites due to “inactive” voting status. The nonprofit newsroom Mississippi Today reported a surge in voter inactivations, which purged more than 200,000 voters from state rolls of registered voters. Inactive voters were permitted to cast provisional or “affidavit” ballots that were still being counted along with absentee ballots in the days after the election.
In one November ad, Colom tied this political moment to the legacy of Civil Rights activist Medgar Evers, a Mississippi native and World War II veteran who returned from the war and was then blocked from registering to vote in Decatur, Mississippi. Evers spent the remainder of his life working to ensure he and other Black citizens would be able to execute that right. He documented voter suppression, helped people register to vote and walked with them to the polls. He also provided civic education in Black gathering spaces throughout the state.
In 1963, a member of the Ku Klux Klan murdered Evers but was not convicted for the killing until 1994.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said in his ad. Evers, who was only 37, “was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” he continued, “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

Democrat Scott Colom will win the U.S. Senate race* in Mississippi, riding a historic wave of turnout to overcome the state’s restrictive voting policies and become its first Black senator since Reconstruction.
His opponent, incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), conceded Wednesday evening.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a video statement.
Earlier, multiple outlets — CNN, VoteHub and the Associated Press — called the race for Colom after affidavit ballots from Hinds County were counted, solidifying his lead over Hyde-Smith.
Colom led by just 4,585 votes when the race was first called, according to the Associated Press.
In a statement, Derrick Johnson, national president of the NAACP, credited Colom’s victory to surging turnout by Black voters.
“In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy,” he said.
“Even in the face of efforts to remove voters from the rolls, attempts to intimidate voters and election officials, and bids to create fear around the electoral process, Mississippi voters showed up,” Johnson continued. “They showed up for their communities, for their families, and for the future of their state. They reminded the nation that we the people have the power.”
National — and international — attention has focused on Mississippi since Election Day, when it became clear Colom appeared poised to unseat Hyde-Smith. Since then, Colom’s lead has been measured in hundreds and thousands of ballots.
In the end, the race came down to affidavit, absentee and mail ballots, many of which are still being counted statewide.
Colom will also be the first Black senator ever to be elected directly by Mississippians — the state’s two previous Black senators were chosen by the legislature in 1870 and 1875.
Beyond its historical significance, Colom’s win represents a major victory over Mississippi’s voting policies, which are among the most restrictive in the nation.
Mississippi does not allow no-excuse mail voting, early voting and same-day and online registration — practices common in many other states with pro-voting policies.
This year, tens of thousands of Mississippians had to vote by affidavit — i.e., provisional — ballot after the state marked them as “inactive” voters following a change in its voter list maintenance procedures.
Even when they did that, there was no guarantee their votes would be counted. On Wednesday, Hinds County, the state’s second most populous county and a Democratic stronghold, rejected roughly two-thirds of its affidavit ballots — most likely for improper registration and votes being cast in the wrong precinct.
The state also makes it harder than most to register to vote: Mississippi requires voters to register through paper applications that they must mail or deliver to county clerks’ offices at least 30 days before an election.
In an interview with Democracy Docket last week, Colom called for sweeping reforms to expand voting access and curb partisan gerrymandering.
*The Elias Law Group (ELG) represents the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and is active in the legal effort on behalf of the Colom campaign. ELG Firm Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.

“Pick another protein?” several incredulous people said in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
During Joe Biden’s presidency, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom from a federal judgeship
Biden nominated Colom, a local prosecutor, to become a U.S. District Court judge for the Northern District of Mississippi.
Colom had backing from Mississippi’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker, and from former Gov. Haley Barbour, a national GOP power broker and former Republican National Committee chairman.
Hyde-Smith, however, invoked her “blue slip” power. That’s Senate lingo for a senator invoking the traditional, unwritten privilege of single-handedly blocking federal court nominees from their home state.
That kind of move has bitten Democrats before, too.
In 1986 then-Alabama Sen. Howell Heflin cast the deciding committee vote — so, technically not a blue slip maneuver — against President Ronald Reagan’s district court nomination of a young U.S. attorney from Alabama named Jeff Sessions.
Ten years later Sessions won a Senate election to succeed Heflin when he retired. In 2017 he became Trump’s first attorney general; Trump later fired him.
Warnock says ‘there’s no going back’
“The people of Mississippi have realized their power and there’s no going back. Scott, welcome to the fight. Let’s get to work,” the Georgia senator posted on social media, along with a photo of himself and Colom campaigning together this fall.
Warnock was elected in a January 2021 runoff to become the first Black U.S. senator from Georgia.
With Colom’s election, there will be three Black U.S. senators from Deep South states in the 120th Congress. The third is Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina.
Warnock was among the early national figures to advocate for Colom and Mississippi as Democrats considered their best opportunities to flip Republican seats and win control of the Senate.
Scott, meanwhile, served as chairman of Senate Republicans’ campaign committee this cycle as Democrats, including Colom, flipped eight GOP-held seats so far. Alaska, where votes are still being tallied, could become the ninth.
Kamala Harris, who made history as vice president, congratulates Colom
“The power is with the people, and the people of Mississippi are with Scott,” the former vice president wrote on social media.
Harris, the first woman and second Black person to hold nationwide office, campaigned for Colom in October and helped him raise money several times during the campaign.
“I saw firsthand when campaigning with him in his hometown that he is a brilliant leader and dedicated public servant who will work tirelessly to serve every Mississippian with pride,” Harris wrote.
Divine Nine Black sororities and fraternities celebrating Colom’s win
One of Colom’s Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity brothers is cheering him on at his victory party.
“He’s a servant, and he’s a leader,” said Tony Howard, who has known Colom for 25 years. He went from “a guy in college sitting around a student table, to now looking at him, that he’s running the world now,” Howard said.
Colom, a Millsaps College alumnus, often would recognize members of the Divine Nine, the historically Black fraternity and sorority organizations in the U.S., at his campaign events.
The organizations have friendly rivalries but come together for civic engagement and philanthropy.
Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Morehouse College alumnus, also is an Alpha Phi Alpha member.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, a Howard University alumna, is in the Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority. Her sorority sisters from campuses across the country often wear their colors — salmon pink and apple green — to her events.
Descendants of enslaved people among those celebrating Colom’s victory
“I am here to celebrate being on the right side of history,” said Vera Finley, as she awaited Colom’s remarks at his victory celebration in Jackson.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley continued. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Finley said Colom’s backers “voted for change” and are “so excited about actually seeing that our votes matter.”
She said she hopes his election yields more unity.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to attend the Group of 20 summit in Florida next month, the State Department said, offering the first confirmation of the visit.
Trump travels to China next week to attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, where the two leaders also are expected to meet.
In a phone call Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi discussed Trump’s “upcoming travel to the APEC summit in China” and Xi’s “upcoming visit to Florida to attend the G20 summit,” the State Department said.
The Chinese foreign ministry’s readout only said the leaders would support each other in hosting the summits.
The State Department said Rubio and Wang also agreed on the importance of the presidents discussing peace and denuclearization, “including at any potential trilateral leaders meeting with Russia.”
Hyde-Smith shares a concession video on social media after calling Colom
The 67-year-old Republican spoke for two minutes, seated next to an American flag.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner, was first appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election and then a full term in 2020.
She said in the video she’s most proud of helping farmers and veterans, opposing abortion rights and securing federal money for Mississippi.
“While my time in the United States Senate may be coming to an end,” she said, “my love for Mississippi and my determination to stand up for what is right never will.”
Why AP called the Mississippi Senate race for Scott Colom
The AP on Wednesday declared Colom the winner in the race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi after several counties reported updated results — including those of last-to-count provisional ballots.
Colom led Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, by 43 votes following the final election night update in Mississippi, which arrived at 3:03 a.m. from Pike County.
Not only has Colom’s lead grown larger as counties in Mississippi have completed their vote count and reported on the outcome of their review of provisional ballots in the days since, but he’s won the vast majority of these final updates — in every region of the state and in all but the most Republican counties — by a large margin.
The AP called the race for the Colom after officials in Jackson County updated their vote count with an additional 2,173 votes.
The update put Colom up by 4,669 votes out of 962,237 counted, or 0.5 percentage points. To come back and take the lead, Hyde-Smith needed to win these final vote updates in GOP-leaning counties such as Jackson. Instead, Colom won the update in Jackson by just over 1 percentage point.
Hyde-Smith has called Colom to concede Mississippi Senate race

She and her advisers previously had not ruled out legal action if the Colom was declared the winner.

The Trump administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new plan presented by the Interior Department.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who will likely chair the House Oversight Committee when Democrats take over next year, said Trump “is clearly hiding something” after the White House issued a warning about their planned probes.

Trump is speaking at Arlington National Cemetery
Trump has told veterans gathered in the amphitheater that service members “are indeed our protection in battle.”

Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, AP source says
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety after spending months executing a massive economic campaign against Iran aimed at severing all of Tehran’s remaining financial ties around the world.
A person familiar with the matter, who spoke to The Associated Press on Wednesday on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details, said the relocation was partly due to media reports that helped identify Bessent’s home address. The relocation was earlier reported by The New York Times.
Other top Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, live on military bases.

The president laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown soldier to honor the nation’s veterans. He’ll also deliver remarks at the amphitheater.
Trump’s motorcade took a different route to the revered burial ground instead of traveling over Memorial Bridge and around a traffic circle where he wants to build a triumphal arch.
Trump’s appearance at the cemetery comes a day after nine Kennedy family members joined several lawsuits seeking to block construction, saying the towering 250-foot (76-meter) arch would cast a shadow over their relatives’ grave sites there.
Rubio speaks with Chinese counterpart before Trump-Xi meeting
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi had a positive and constructive phone talk with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, Chinese state media reported.
Trump is set to travel to Asia next week and meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Wang told Rubio that China is willing to strengthen communications and cooperation with the U.S. and properly handle differences and sensitive issues.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent extolled the U.S.-China bond as “one of this century’s most consequential relationships” at a Tuesday night gala in New York with Chinese ambassador to the U.S. Xie Feng.
Mississippi’s Senate seat remains too early to call
Democrat Scott Colom was about 3,000 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday with 98% of the votes counted.
Tuesday was the deadline for receiving mail-in absentee ballots. Counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday. It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
The AP may declare a winner if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Black Democrat Scott Colom Wins Mississippi Senate Race
In what will likely go down as one of the most historic moments in Mississippi history, Democrat Scott Colom has beaten incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for the U.S. Senate seat.
CNN projects Colom to be the winner of the race, making him the state’s first Democratic Senator in four decades and the first Black senator since Reconstruction.
This is yet another Black wave in the blue tsunami that took over a little over a week ago, when Democrats celebrated strong wins, gaining control of both the House and the Senate, and electing Black governors across the country as well.
Colom’s victory includes the fact that he flipped Forrest County, a Republican stronghold named after the founder of the Ku Klux Klan.
From CNN:
Colom campaigned relentlessly as he sought to energize Black voters, who make up roughly 35% of the state’s electorate. He also worked to build a coalition that includes White, working-class Mississippians.
The win comes just a few years after Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination to the federal bench, although the Democrat had the backing of other Republicans, including Sen. Roger Wicker, Mississippi’s senior senator.
Hyde-Smith became the first female US senator from Mississippi when she was appointed in 2018 to fill a vacancy. She went on to win a special election later that year and reelection in 2020.
The Associated Press is also calling the race for Colom, noting that “Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.”
As NewsOne previously reported, by “midday Tuesday, Colom maintained a 2,536-vote advantage over Hyde-Smith in the unofficial tally, according to the Associated Press. But two important deadlines arrived Tuesday afternoon that could affect the outcome: resolving provisional ballots cast because of questions about voters’ eligibility and receiving mail-in absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day.”
Once those votes are accounted for, officials in all 82 Mississippi counties have until the close of business Friday to certify their election results.
And there is plenty riding on those remaining ballots.
The largest number of outstanding votes Tuesday were in Hinds County, a Democratic stronghold surrounding the state capital of Jackson, with another significant batch remaining in neighboring Holmes County, which is even more reliably blue. The geographic distribution of those outstanding votes has continued to favor Colom, the Washington Post reports.
This is a major victory for a Black man in what Mother Jones refers to as a state that was “once the epicenter of Jim Crow.”
More from Mother Jones:
This was the state where Jim Crow was the most violent and repressive. It was where Emmett Till was lynched, Evers was assassinated, and the young civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan. There were 581 documented lynchings during the Jim Crow era, more than any other state.
“Just to mention Mississippi, to cross the state line from Alabama and go there, it just created all types of problems in my own mind,” the late congressman and civil rights activist John Lewis once said. “It seemed like when you just drove over the state line, something happened to the air, to the environment. It was a psychological thing… Alabama is bad; Alabama is hell. But to go to Mississippi at the time was worse than hell.”
Change doesn’t always come quickly or loudly, but it shows up at just the right time.
Scott Colom is just the right man at the right time.
Over here at NewsOne, we are proud of Senator-elect Colom and congratulate him on his well-earned victory.

Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
Summary
Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race after several days of ballot counting, making him the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. The Associated Press called the race for Colom on Wednesday after officials processed absentee and provisional ballots. His victory came amid a broader midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump’s party and drew attention to Democrats’ prospects in the South. Colom, a local prosecutor, campaigned on representing voters across Mississippi.
Key Facts
- Colom is 43 and serves as a local prosecutor.
- Mississippi last elected a new Democratic senator in 1947; that winner was a segregationist.
- Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 after Thad Cochran resigned, won a special-election runoff that year and secured a full term in 2020.
- In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship, but Hyde-Smith blocked his confirmation.
- Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024, while Republican Gov. Tate Reeves won reelection in 2023 by 3 percentage points.
JACKSON, Miss. — Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43 year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don’t come up with excuses as to why we can’t do it,” he said.
A race Washington once viewed as a longshot
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy. The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.
Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
“I love that,” Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. “Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes.”
The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.
Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi's history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom's bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.
Despite Republicans' domination, path was always there
With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”

sources.news_title: Democrat Scott Colom Flips US Senate Seat in Mississippi
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney in eastern Mississippi, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Nov. 3 election, flipping a Senate seat Republicans had held since 1978.
The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 11 for Colom.
With 99 percent of the votes counted, The Associated Press said that Colom had 49.2 percent of the vote to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7 percent. Colom had 473,336 votes and Hyde-Smith had 468,667 votes.
Independent Ty Pinkins had 2.1 percent of the vote, or 20,234 votes.
Hyde-Smith posted on Nov. 11 on X, “Thank you, Mississippi.”
In a video, Hyde-Smith said the outcome wasn’t what her campaign worked and hoped for.
“I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said, while congratulating Colom.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, congratulated Colom on the victory Wednesday.
“Congratulations to Senator-Elect Colom on his historic win and on becoming the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat in over four decades,” the lawmakers said in a statement. “We will work hand in hand with Scott to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress and look forward to welcoming him to our caucus.”
Colom is the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate election in Mississippi since Sen. John Stennis won his final term in 1982.
Colom held just a 43-vote lead after the early midterm counts with more than 945,000 votes cast.
Hyde-Smith was seeking a second full term. She was appointed to the Senate in April 2018 after Republican Sen. Thad Cochran stepped down in 2018 because of health concerns. Hyde-Smith won a special election that November to serve the rest of his term.
In 2020, she won a full term with 54.1 percent of the vote, defeating Democrat Mike Espy by about 10 percentage points.
Colom drew late support from national Democrats, as the Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million television ad buy and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for him in his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi.
Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Democratic-aligned super PAC, had said the ads would run through Election Day on Nov. 3 and would mark the group’s first spending in the race. The investment came as the Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the contest from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”
Harris addressed about 1,000 people at Columbus High School on Oct. 22, urging voters to “turn that anger into action.”
The Hyde-Smith campaign pointed out how long it took for the Democrats to spend money supporting Colom’s campaign.
“It took [Senate Minority Leader] Chuck Schumer [D-N.Y.] and his Super PACs 13 months to run a single ad for Scott Colom,” Nathan Calvert, communications director for the Hyde-Smith campaign, said in an email to The Epoch Times.
“Chuck knows what Mississippians know, Scott Colom is too liberal, he supports transgender surgeries for children, men in women’s restrooms and locker rooms, open borders, and higher taxes.”
The Democrats said they believed early in 2025 that they could compete in Mississippi, French said on X.
“None of this came out of nowhere. Democrats have talked about Mississippi all cycle,” French said. “Most notably Leader Schumer, who has made the case since the early days of 2025 that Democrats can and should compete in Mississippi.”

Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes.
Loading...
In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.
Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction.
The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.
Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.
Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.
"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."
Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.
When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."
That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."

sources.news_title: Scott Colom becomes Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
sources.text:
Scott Colom defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s US Senate race to become the state’s first Black senator since the end of the American Civil War and Reconstruction.
After days of tallying ballots, the Associated Press called the race for Colom in the historically Republican state on Wednesday.
His win was seen as a major political achievement in the heavily Republican state of Mississippi. It also contributed to Democratic gains in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when the GOP was hit with widespread losses.
“All I did was to have the courage to envision a night like this,” Colom said to cheers and applause at his celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson.
Colom made an economic message focusing on the rising cost of living and attempted to appeal to voters outside of the Democratic Party. He was endorsed by prominent Democratic leaders including former President Bill Clinton and ex-Vice President Kamala Harris.
Hyde-Smith formally conceded Wednesday and extended congratulations to Colom, stating she respected the decision of the people of Mississippi.
Reuters also notes that Colom’s success means he will be the first Democrat elected to a Mississippi Senate seat since 1982.
